4.1.title: Context and external issues
4.1.objective: Understand which conditions affect the ISMS and whether climate change matters to its outcomes.

questions.prompt: Have you identified internal conditions that affect the ISMS's intended outcomes?
questions.help: Consider how strategy, staffing, culture, technology and working arrangements affect security. Discuss the conditions relevant to this organization's purpose, rather than copying a generic list.
questions.remediation: Identify purpose-relevant internal conditions affecting ISMS outcomes.

questions.prompt: Have you identified external conditions that affect the ISMS's intended outcomes?
questions.help: Consider relevant market, legal, supplier, social and technical conditions. A workshop, existing business analysis or another suitable approach can support the decision; a separate context register is optional.
questions.remediation: Identify purpose-relevant external conditions affecting ISMS outcomes.

questions.prompt: Has the organization decided whether climate change is relevant to the ISMS?
questions.help: Consider effects on information security and the ISMS, such as service dependencies or changing obligations. A considered conclusion that climate change is not relevant can satisfy this inquiry; ignoring the question cannot. This does not require a separate environmental program.
questions.topic: Context and external issues: climate decision
questions.remediation: Determine whether climate change is relevant to ISMS outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which context decision would help explain these answers? (Optional)
questions.help: Describe a useful example if available. A missing example, document title or contact name does not change reported status.
questions.topic: Context and external issues: context note

4.2.title: Stakeholder obligations
4.2.objective: Understand relevant parties, their requirements and the organization's decision about what the ISMS addresses.

questions.prompt: Have you identified the interested parties that matter to this ISMS?
questions.help: Consider relevant customers, workers, regulators, owners and providers. The appropriate set depends on the in-scope activities; these are examples, not a prescribed roster.
questions.remediation: Identify interested parties relevant to the ISMS.

questions.prompt: Have you determined which requirements from those parties are relevant?
questions.help: Consider actual legal, regulatory and contractual obligations and other relevant expectations. Include climate-related requirements where relevant: the 2024 note highlights that possibility without requiring every party to have one.
questions.remediation: Determine the relevant requirements of identified interested parties.

questions.prompt: Is it clear which of those requirements the ISMS will address?
questions.help: Explain the organization's choices using actual requirements and scope. An obligation register, agreements or another understandable record can support the answer; this interview does not determine legal applicability.
questions.remediation: Determine which relevant interested-party requirements the ISMS addresses.

4.3.title: ISMS boundaries
4.3.objective: Understand the scope, the decisions behind its boundaries and whether people can retrieve it.

questions.prompt: Is it clear which parts of the organization and activities the ISMS covers?
questions.help: Explain the boundary in terms that fit actual services, information, locations and responsibilities. Defining a limited organizational scope does not permit excluding mandatory ISMS clauses within that scope.
questions.remediation: Determine understandable ISMS boundaries and applicability.

questions.prompt: Did scope decisions take the identified internal and external conditions into account?
questions.help: Trace relevant context decisions, including climate relevance where applicable, into the boundary. A diagram is optional; the reasoning matters.
questions.remediation: Consider organizational context when determining scope.

questions.prompt: Did scope decisions take relevant interested-party requirements into account?
questions.help: Use the actual requirements identified under 4.2, including relevant contractual interfaces. Do not infer scope from a framework label alone.
questions.remediation: Consider interested-party requirements when determining scope.

questions.prompt: Were interfaces and dependencies with other organizations considered when setting the scope?
questions.help: Consider hosted services, shared functions and information exchanges. Outsourcing does not remove an in-scope dependency; different arrangements may explain how it is handled.
questions.remediation: Consider interfaces and dependencies with other organizations.

questions.prompt: Can the current ISMS scope be retrieved as documented information?
questions.help: A controlled page, approved description or another suitable record can work. No particular file name or boundary-diagram format is required.
questions.remediation: Make the ISMS scope available as documented information.

4.4.title: ISMS processes
4.4.objective: Understand whether the ISMS exists as connected, operating and improving processes.

questions.prompt: Have the processes needed for this ISMS been established?
questions.help: Describe the organization's actual risk, treatment, evaluation and improvement work. Reuse existing business processes where they meet the need; a new process library is optional.
questions.remediation: Establish the processes needed for the ISMS.

questions.prompt: Are the interactions between those processes established?
questions.help: Explain a handoff, such as a risk decision informing treatment and management review. A process map is one possible explanation, not a required artifact.
questions.remediation: Establish the necessary ISMS process interactions.

questions.prompt: Are those processes used to implement the ISMS?
questions.help: Describe how the management system works in practice against its requirements. Document presence alone does not demonstrate implementation.
questions.remediation: Implement the established ISMS processes.

questions.prompt: Is the ISMS maintained as the organization operates?
questions.help: Discuss how existing processes continue to work and remain usable. Do not invent a universal annual review cycle.
questions.remediation: Maintain the ISMS and its processes.

questions.prompt: Is the organization continually improving the ISMS?
questions.help: Describe improvements to how the management system works. Existing review, corrective-action and change processes may provide the mechanism.
questions.remediation: Continually improve the ISMS.

5.1.title: Leadership accountability
5.1.objective: Understand how top management provides direction, support and accountability for ISMS outcomes.

questions.prompt: Has top management ensured that an information security policy is established?
questions.help: Describe management's involvement in establishing policy direction. A sponsor's name alone is insufficient, and no specific committee is required.
questions.remediation: Ensure leadership establishes information security policy direction.

questions.prompt: Has top management ensured that security objectives are established?
questions.help: Use the organization's actual objectives, rather than a generic list of suggested targets.
questions.remediation: Ensure leadership establishes security objectives.

questions.prompt: Do leadership's policy and objective decisions fit the organization's strategic direction?
questions.help: Explain how priorities reflect the organization's purpose and strategy. The standard does not prescribe a particular strategy document.
questions.remediation: Align security policy and objectives with organizational direction.

questions.prompt: Has leadership integrated ISMS requirements into relevant business processes?
questions.help: Consider operational decisions and responsibilities where security requirements matter. Existing planning and approval processes can support this.
questions.remediation: Integrate ISMS requirements into relevant organizational processes.

questions.prompt: Does leadership ensure that the ISMS resources it needs are available?
questions.help: Discuss actual time, capability and other resources needed to carry out ISMS work. A dedicated department or software platform is not inherently required.
questions.remediation: Ensure needed ISMS resources are available.

questions.prompt: Does leadership communicate why effective security management and meeting ISMS requirements matter?
questions.help: Consider messages people actually receive and understand. Meetings, written direction or other appropriate communications can work.
questions.remediation: Communicate the importance of effective security management and ISMS requirements.

questions.prompt: Does leadership ensure that the ISMS achieves its intended outcomes?
questions.help: Describe how management notices shortfalls and acts on them. Having a dashboard without management attention is insufficient.
questions.remediation: Ensure leadership follows through on intended ISMS outcomes.

questions.prompt: Does leadership direct and support people contributing to ISMS effectiveness?
questions.help: Discuss actual support for people doing security-related work; this can be practical direction and problem resolution.
questions.remediation: Direct and support people's contribution to ISMS effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Does leadership support other relevant managers in their security responsibilities?
questions.help: Consider how managers receive authority and support in their own areas. No particular management hierarchy is required.
questions.remediation: Support relevant managers in demonstrating security leadership.

questions.prompt: Does leadership promote continual ISMS improvement?
questions.help: Describe how management encourages useful changes and acts on improvement opportunities. A separate improvement committee is optional.
questions.remediation: Promote continual improvement of the ISMS.

5.2.title: Security policy direction
5.2.objective: Understand management's security direction, its commitments and how it reaches relevant people.

questions.prompt: Has top management established a security policy suited to the organization's purpose?
questions.help: Consider the organization's actual activities and priorities. A generic template can be adapted, but its title alone does not establish suitability.
questions.remediation: Establish a security policy appropriate to organizational purpose.

questions.prompt: Does the policy include security objectives or provide a usable basis for setting them?
questions.help: Either approach can work. Objectives may be maintained separately when the policy gives a meaningful framework for them.
questions.remediation: Include objectives or a framework for setting security objectives.

questions.prompt: Does the policy commit the organization to meeting applicable information security requirements?
questions.help: Consider the actual direction expressed in the policy; this interview does not decide which laws apply.
questions.remediation: Include commitment to applicable information security requirements.

questions.prompt: Does the policy commit the organization to continually improving the ISMS?
questions.help: Check management's stated direction. A particular policy title or declaration template is not required.
questions.remediation: Include commitment to continual ISMS improvement.

questions.prompt: Is the security policy available as documented information?
questions.help: An accessible controlled policy page or another suitable format can work. A signed paper file is not the only option.
questions.remediation: Make the information security policy available as documented information.

questions.prompt: Has the policy been communicated within the organization?
questions.help: Explain how affected people receive the current direction. An awareness platform or annual acknowledgement is not required by this question.
questions.remediation: Communicate the security policy within the organization.

questions.prompt: Is the policy available to interested parties where appropriate?
questions.help: Use actual relationship needs. Controlled sharing or a suitable published version can be appropriate; making the full internal policy public is not universally required.
questions.remediation: Make the policy appropriately available to interested parties.

5.3.title: Accountable ISMS roles
5.3.objective: Understand assigned security duties, authority and reporting without requiring specific job titles.

questions.prompt: Has top management assigned relevant information security responsibilities and authority?
questions.help: Describe what roles are expected and empowered to do. One person may hold several compatible duties; no job title or RACI format is prescribed.
questions.remediation: Assign relevant security responsibilities and authority.

questions.prompt: Have those assignments been communicated within the organization?
questions.help: People should understand the duties and decision authority relevant to their work. Role descriptions, conversations or another appropriate route can work.
questions.remediation: Communicate relevant security responsibilities and authority.

questions.prompt: Has management assigned responsibility and authority for ensuring ISMS conformity?
questions.help: Identify the assigned duty and authority. The role need not be called CISO or ISO officer, and the interview is not a conformity opinion.
questions.remediation: Assign responsibility and authority for ISMS conformity.

questions.prompt: Has management assigned responsibility and authority for reporting ISMS performance to top management?
questions.help: Explain the reporting responsibility and how it reaches management. This does not require a specific reporting product.
questions.remediation: Assign responsibility and authority for reporting ISMS performance.

questions.prompt: Which role or contact can help explain the assignments? (Optional)
questions.help: A missing contact name does not change status. The substantive questions separately assess whether responsibility and authority are assigned.

6.1.1.title: Planning risks and opportunities
6.1.1.objective: Understand how context-informed planning addresses uncertainty and makes actions and evaluation workable.

questions.prompt: Does ISMS planning consider the internal and external context identified under 4.1?
questions.help: Trace a relevant business condition into planning. Climate relevance can be one input, without implying a separate climate-control program.
questions.remediation: Use organizational context in ISMS planning.

questions.prompt: Does ISMS planning consider the relevant requirements identified under 4.2?
questions.help: Use actual interested-party requirements, not assumed obligations based on a client label.
questions.remediation: Use relevant interested-party requirements in ISMS planning.

questions.prompt: Have you determined which risks need attention in planning the ISMS?
questions.help: Consider risks to the management system's ability to work as intended. This complements the information-security risk method in 6.1.2.
questions.remediation: Determine risks requiring attention in ISMS planning.

questions.prompt: Have you determined which opportunities need attention in planning the ISMS?
questions.help: Consider useful opportunities to strengthen the management system. A separate opportunity register or invented project is optional.
questions.remediation: Determine opportunities requiring attention in ISMS planning.

questions.prompt: Do those risk and opportunity choices support the ISMS's intended outcomes?
questions.help: Explain what success the planning choices protect. The organization's actual intended outcomes provide the reference.
questions.remediation: Address risks and opportunities needed for intended ISMS outcomes.

questions.prompt: Do the choices address prevention or reduction of unwanted effects?
questions.help: Explain the effects planning is intended to prevent or reduce. Eliminating every possible risk is not implied.
questions.remediation: Address prevention or reduction of unwanted effects.

questions.prompt: Do the choices address continual ISMS improvement?
questions.help: Discuss how the planned response supports improvement, without assuming a particular improvement project.
questions.remediation: Address risks and opportunities needed for continual improvement.

questions.prompt: Have actions been planned for the selected risks and opportunities?
questions.help: Describe a practicable response using existing plans or work records. This asks about chosen actions, not a prescribed plan template.
questions.remediation: Plan actions addressing selected risks and opportunities.

questions.prompt: Have you planned how those actions fit into the ISMS processes?
questions.help: Explain the connection to existing operational or management activities. A standalone action list without an integration plan leaves this unclear.
questions.remediation: Plan integration of the actions into ISMS processes.

questions.prompt: Have you planned how those actions will be carried out?
questions.help: Describe the organization's intended delivery approach. A new project-management product is optional.
questions.remediation: Plan implementation of the actions through the ISMS.

questions.prompt: Have you planned how the effectiveness of those actions will be evaluated?
questions.help: Explain what would show the response worked. Fixed monthly, quarterly or annual intervals are not introduced here.
questions.remediation: Plan evaluation of the actions' effectiveness.

6.1.2.title: Risk assessment method
6.1.2.objective: Understand whether the risk method supports repeatable, meaningful decisions about in-scope information.

questions.prompt: Is an information security risk-assessment process defined?
questions.help: Explain the steps assessors follow. A qualitative, quantitative or mixed approach may work when it supports the required decisions.
questions.remediation: Define the information security risk-assessment process.

questions.prompt: Is that process actually applied to risk assessments?
questions.help: Compare the method with completed assessments. Buying a risk tool or approving a method without using it is insufficient.
questions.remediation: Apply the defined risk-assessment process.

questions.prompt: Is documented information about the assessment process retained?
questions.help: An accessible procedure or equivalent controlled record can work. A particular methodology name is optional.
questions.remediation: Retain documented information about the risk-assessment process.

questions.prompt: Are criteria for accepting information security risk established?
questions.help: Explain how acceptable and unacceptable risk are distinguished. A numeric threshold is one option, not a universal requirement.
questions.remediation: Establish information security risk-acceptance criteria.

questions.prompt: Are the risk-acceptance criteria maintained?
questions.help: Explain how the adopted criteria remain usable for current decisions. No universal review interval is prescribed here.
questions.remediation: Maintain information security risk-acceptance criteria.

questions.prompt: Are criteria for performing risk assessments established?
questions.help: Explain the agreed basis for assessors' decisions, such as scales or evaluation rules appropriate to the organization.
questions.remediation: Establish criteria for performing information security risk assessments.

questions.prompt: Are those assessment criteria maintained?
questions.help: Discuss whether current assessments still use appropriate criteria. Replacing criteria without understanding earlier results may undermine comparison.
questions.remediation: Maintain the criteria for performing risk assessments.

questions.prompt: Does repeated use of the method produce consistent results?
questions.help: Consider whether assessors apply the agreed criteria in a consistent way. Examples or calibration discussions can help explain the answer.
questions.remediation: Resolve inconsistency in repeated risk assessments.

questions.prompt: Does the method produce results that represent the risks being assessed?
questions.help: Consider whether judgments are grounded in actual circumstances and meaningful criteria. Automated scores are not automatically valid.
questions.remediation: Resolve weaknesses affecting the validity of risk-assessment results.

questions.prompt: Can results from repeated assessments be meaningfully compared?
questions.help: Explain how changes in assumptions or criteria are understood when comparing results. No specific risk-scoring system is required.
questions.remediation: Make repeated risk-assessment results meaningfully comparable.

questions.prompt: Does risk identification consider loss of confidentiality of in-scope information?
questions.help: Consider inappropriate access or disclosure using actual information and relationships. An asset-first or scenario-first method can both work.
questions.remediation: Identify confidentiality-loss risks to in-scope information.

questions.prompt: Does risk identification consider loss of integrity of in-scope information?
questions.help: Consider unwanted alteration, corruption or loss of trust in information. Do not assume every risk is only a cyberattack.
questions.remediation: Identify integrity-loss risks to in-scope information.

questions.prompt: Does risk identification consider loss of availability of in-scope information?
questions.help: Consider inability to access needed information or services. Use the organization's actual service dependencies.
questions.remediation: Identify availability-loss risks to in-scope information.

questions.prompt: Does risk identification cover information throughout the ISMS scope?
questions.help: Consider important interfaces and externally provided services as well as internal activities. A limited assessment sample does not define the whole scope.
questions.remediation: Cover in-scope information in risk identification.

questions.prompt: Are owners identified for the information security risks?
questions.help: Explain who is responsible for each risk. An individual or appropriate accountable role can work; an optional contact name is not the duty being assessed.
questions.remediation: Identify the owners of information security risks.

questions.prompt: Are potential consequences assessed for identified risks?
questions.help: Use the possible effects on the organization if the scenario occurs. A qualitative impact description can be suitable.
questions.remediation: Assess potential consequences of identified risks.

questions.prompt: Is realistic likelihood assessed for identified risks?
questions.help: Explain assumptions using actual conditions and available information. A precise probability is not inherently required.
questions.remediation: Assess realistic likelihood of identified risks.

questions.prompt: Are risk levels determined from the analysis?
questions.help: Explain how the organization's method produces the level used for decisions. A particular scoring formula is optional.
questions.remediation: Determine risk levels using the adopted analysis method.

questions.prompt: Are analysis results compared with the established risk criteria?
questions.help: Explain how the comparison informs a decision about the assessed risk. A score without evaluation does not answer this question.
questions.remediation: Compare analyzed risks with established risk criteria.

questions.prompt: Are analyzed risks prioritized for treatment?
questions.help: Describe how the evaluation determines attention or sequence. The interview does not impose a specific ordering formula.
questions.remediation: Prioritize analyzed risks for treatment.

6.1.3.title: Treatment decisions and SoA
6.1.3.objective: Understand how treatment choices lead to necessary controls, justified SoA decisions and risk-owner approval.

questions.prompt: Is an information security risk-treatment process defined?
questions.help: Explain how assessed risks lead to treatment decisions. Use the existing risk workflow where appropriate.
questions.remediation: Define the information security risk-treatment process.

questions.prompt: Is that process applied to treatment decisions?
questions.help: Trace an actual decision from assessment to treatment. A plan template without use does not demonstrate application.
questions.remediation: Apply the defined risk-treatment process.

questions.prompt: Are appropriate treatment options selected using the risk-assessment results?
questions.help: Different responses can be appropriate for different risks. Do not equate acceptance with automatic completion of every control.
questions.remediation: Select appropriate treatment options using assessment results.

questions.prompt: Have all controls needed for the chosen treatment options been determined?
questions.help: Consider controls designed by the organization or selected from any suitable source. Necessary controls can extend beyond Annex A.
questions.remediation: Determine the controls necessary for chosen treatments.

questions.prompt: Have those necessary controls been compared with Annex A?
questions.help: The comparison is a safeguard against omissions; it does not make every Annex A control universally necessary. Existing mapping records can support it.
questions.topic: Treatment decisions and SoA: annex comparison
questions.remediation: Compare necessary controls with the Annex A reference set.

questions.prompt: Has the comparison been used to check that necessary controls were not missed?
questions.help: Explain how unmatched reference controls or treatment gaps were considered. A completed mapping alone does not establish that omissions were evaluated.
questions.remediation: Check the comparison for omitted necessary controls.

questions.prompt: Does the SoA identify the necessary controls, including additional controls when needed?
questions.help: Use the organization's selected controls, including custom or non-Annex controls. An Annex-only list can omit necessary treatments.
questions.topic: Treatment decisions and SoA: SoA controls
questions.remediation: Include necessary controls in the Statement of Applicability.

questions.prompt: Does the SoA explain why its necessary controls are included?
questions.help: Reasons may reflect risk, obligations or other relevant needs. Presence in Annex A alone is not the organization's treatment rationale.
questions.topic: Treatment decisions and SoA: SoA inclusion
questions.remediation: Record justification for including necessary controls.

questions.prompt: Does the SoA state whether the necessary controls are implemented?
questions.help: Keep implementation state separate from selection and exclusion decisions. Evidence links alone do not decide implementation.
questions.topic: Treatment decisions and SoA: SoA implementation
questions.remediation: Record whether the necessary controls are implemented.

questions.prompt: Are any excluded Annex A controls justified in the SoA?
questions.help: If none are excluded, explain that position; do not invent an exclusion. If there are exclusions, each needs a reason based on the organization's circumstances. No answer changes whole-clause applicability.
questions.topic: Treatment decisions and SoA: SoA exclusions
questions.remediation: Justify any excluded Annex A controls in the SoA.

questions.prompt: Has an information security risk-treatment plan been formulated?
questions.help: An integrated plan or linked treatment records can work when they provide the needed plan. A particular plan title or project tool is optional.
questions.remediation: Formulate an information security risk-treatment plan.

questions.prompt: Have the risk owners approved the treatment plan?
questions.help: Check the owners' actual approval through the organization's appropriate process. Top management review alone does not substitute for risk-owner approval.
questions.remediation: Obtain risk-owner approval of the treatment plan.

questions.prompt: Have the risk owners accepted the residual information security risks?
questions.help: Discuss the remaining exposure and the owners' actual acceptance decision. A completed treatment action does not itself record residual-risk acceptance.
questions.topic: Treatment decisions and SoA: residual acceptance
questions.remediation: Obtain risk-owner acceptance of residual information security risks.

questions.prompt: Is documented information about the treatment process retained?
questions.help: Use a controlled procedure or equivalent record. This is separate from the results retained under 8.3.
questions.remediation: Retain documented information about the risk-treatment process.

6.2.title: Measurable security objectives
6.2.objective: Understand appropriate objectives and the delivery and evaluation arrangements supporting them.

questions.prompt: Are security objectives established at the relevant functions and levels?
questions.help: Use objectives appropriate to where work and decisions occur. Every team does not need a separate objective if that level is not relevant.
questions.remediation: Establish security objectives at relevant functions and levels.

questions.prompt: Are those objectives consistent with the security policy?
questions.help: Explain how objectives reflect the adopted policy direction. A generic target list does not demonstrate that connection.
questions.remediation: Align objectives with information security policy.

questions.prompt: Are the objectives measurable wherever that is practicable?
questions.help: Use measures suited to the objective. Where measurement is impracticable, explain why and how achievement can be evaluated; a numeric KPI is not universally required.
questions.remediation: Make objectives measurable where practicable.

questions.prompt: Do objectives take applicable security requirements into account?
questions.help: Use actual obligations and requirements determined for the organization. Do not infer legal applicability from an interview answer.
questions.remediation: Consider applicable security requirements when setting objectives.

questions.prompt: Do objectives take risk-assessment results into account?
questions.help: Trace relevant assessed exposures into the chosen objectives where appropriate.
questions.remediation: Consider risk-assessment results when setting objectives.

questions.prompt: Do objectives take risk-treatment results into account?
questions.help: Consider the treatment decisions and remaining exposures affecting intended outcomes.
questions.remediation: Consider risk-treatment results when setting objectives.

questions.prompt: Are the objectives monitored?
questions.help: Explain how progress is observed using suitable information. A dashboard is one option, and no universal monitoring interval is prescribed here.
questions.remediation: Monitor the security objectives.

questions.prompt: Are the objectives communicated to relevant people?
questions.help: Consider the people who need to understand or contribute to the objectives. Existing meetings or written direction can work.
questions.remediation: Communicate the security objectives.

questions.prompt: Are the objectives updated when appropriate?
questions.help: Explain how the organization responds when objectives need to change. An annual rewrite is not inherently required.
questions.remediation: Update security objectives as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Are the objectives available as documented information?
questions.help: A controlled page, plan or another suitable record can work. A dedicated objectives register is optional.
questions.remediation: Make objectives available as documented information.

questions.prompt: Is documented information about the objectives retained?
questions.help: Explain how records remain available rather than being lost as objectives change. This does not invent a retention period.
questions.remediation: Retain documented information about the objectives.

questions.prompt: Does achievement planning identify what will be done?
questions.help: Explain the planned work supporting the objective, using existing plans where suitable.
questions.remediation: Determine the work needed to achieve each objective.

questions.prompt: Does achievement planning identify required resources?
questions.help: Consider the actual people, time, capabilities and other resources needed; a specific tool is optional.
questions.remediation: Determine the resources needed to achieve each objective.

questions.prompt: Does achievement planning identify who is responsible?
questions.help: Identify responsibility for delivery. The label of the role is flexible; responsibility itself is substantive.
questions.remediation: Determine responsibility for achieving each objective.

questions.prompt: Does achievement planning identify when the work will be completed?
questions.help: Use a completion timeframe appropriate to the objective. The standard does not impose an identical deadline for all objectives.
questions.remediation: Determine completion timing for objective achievement work.

questions.prompt: Does achievement planning identify how the results will be evaluated?
questions.help: Explain how the organization will judge success. Finishing activities alone does not show whether an objective was achieved.
questions.remediation: Determine how objective results will be evaluated.

6.3.title: Planned ISMS changes
6.3.objective: Understand how needed ISMS changes are planned without treating an event-free period as clause exclusion.

questions.prompt: Is there a workable approach for planning changes when the ISMS needs to change?
questions.help: Describe how an identified change would be planned before execution. An existing change process can work; no dedicated ISMS change tool, approval board or mandatory impact template is introduced. This question remains present if no change has occurred.
questions.remediation: Establish a workable approach for planning identified ISMS changes.

questions.prompt: Were any needed ISMS changes identified in the period being discussed?
questions.help: Choose Not relevant here only if no needed change was identified, and give the reason. This scopes the execution example only; the planning question and mandatory clause remain.
questions.remediation: Confirm whether a needed ISMS change was identified.

questions.prompt: Were the identified changes carried out in a planned way?
questions.help: Use an actual change to scope, processes or management-system arrangements. Existing planning records or equivalent evidence can explain what happened; no fixed project template is required.
questions.remediation: Carry out identified ISMS changes in a planned manner.

7.1.title: ISMS resources
7.1.objective: Understand which resources the ISMS needs and whether they are provided.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined the resources needed to run and improve the ISMS?
questions.help: Consider the actual workload, capability, time and infrastructure needed for establishment, operation, upkeep and improvement. Existing business resource planning can be used.
questions.remediation: Determine the resources needed for the ISMS.

questions.prompt: Are those needed resources provided?
questions.help: Describe how the organization makes the necessary capacity available. Internal staff, shared services or appropriate external support can work. No particular software, dedicated security team or budget format is inherently required.
questions.remediation: Provide the resources needed for the ISMS.

questions.prompt: Which existing tools or working arrangements help provide those resources? (Optional)
questions.help: Record useful context if known. Tool names, spending figures and contact names are optional and do not determine status.

7.2.title: Role competence
7.2.objective: Understand how relevant people have the capability to perform their security-related work.

questions.prompt: Have competence needs been determined for people whose work affects information security performance?
questions.help: Consider people working under the organization's control, including relevant contractors. Duties may include risk assessment, operations or audit; these are examples, not a required role list.
questions.remediation: Determine competence needs for work affecting information security performance.

questions.prompt: Is competence established for those people on an appropriate basis?
questions.help: Education, training or experience can support competence. Assess what the work needs; a certificate or course attendance is not the only acceptable route.
questions.remediation: Ensure relevant people have the necessary competence.

questions.prompt: Can the organization take action where competence needs to be acquired or strengthened?
questions.help: Explain the existing approach. Training, mentoring, reassignment or engaging competent people can be alternatives; no particular training product is required. This question remains even when no gap has been found.
questions.remediation: Arrange appropriate action when competence needs support.

questions.prompt: Were actions needed to establish or strengthen competence in the period discussed?
questions.help: Choose Not relevant here only if no such action was needed, and explain why. This scopes action examples without excluding the competence obligations.
questions.remediation: Confirm whether competence-support actions were needed.

questions.prompt: Were appropriate actions taken to address the identified competence needs?
questions.help: Discuss the selected action and the person's actual needs. Equivalent ways to gain competence can work; course attendance alone is not the required outcome.
questions.remediation: Take appropriate action to meet identified competence needs.

questions.prompt: Was the effectiveness of those competence actions evaluated?
questions.help: Explain what showed that the action improved capability for the relevant work. A practical demonstration, supervision or another suitable assessment can work.
questions.remediation: Evaluate whether competence actions achieved their purpose.

questions.prompt: Is suitable documented information retained to support competence?
questions.help: Use relevant experience, qualification, assessment or training records as appropriate. A competence matrix and a specific certificate are examples, not universal required artifacts.
questions.remediation: Retain suitable documented information supporting competence.

7.3.title: Workforce awareness
7.3.objective: Understand what people working under organizational control know about the ISMS and their contribution.

questions.prompt: Are relevant people aware of the information security policy?
questions.help: Consider people working under the organization's control. Check understanding appropriate to their work; an awareness platform or annual acknowledgement is optional.
questions.remediation: Make relevant people aware of information security policy.

questions.prompt: Are those people aware of how their work contributes to ISMS effectiveness?
questions.help: Ask what they do that supports the management system. Course completion alone does not explain their contribution.
questions.remediation: Build awareness of each person's contribution to ISMS effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Are those people aware of the benefits of improved information security performance?
questions.help: Use benefits relevant to actual work and outcomes, such as dependable service or reduced mistakes. No scripted awareness message is required.
questions.remediation: Build awareness of the benefits of improved security performance.

questions.prompt: Are those people aware of the implications of not meeting ISMS requirements?
questions.help: Explain appropriate consequences and effects in the organization's context. This does not mandate a particular disciplinary policy or penalty.
questions.remediation: Build awareness of the implications of departing from ISMS requirements.

7.4.title: ISMS communications
7.4.objective: Understand what ISMS communication is needed and its audience, timing and method.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined what internal and external ISMS information needs to be communicated?
questions.help: Use actual needs such as policy direction or performance information. Examples do not create a universal list of notices.
questions.remediation: Determine the needed subject matter of ISMS communications.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined when those communications are needed?
questions.help: Events or planned timing can both be appropriate. Do not assume all communications require an annual or quarterly schedule.
questions.remediation: Determine when needed ISMS communications occur.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined the intended internal and external recipients?
questions.help: Use the actual relationships and information needs. Outsourcing does not imply that all communication duties disappear.
questions.remediation: Determine the audiences for needed ISMS communications.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined how those communications will be delivered?
questions.help: Suitable meetings, written messages, shared pages or other routes may work. The 2022 comparison identifies how to communicate; it does not prescribe a communication platform.
questions.remediation: Determine suitable methods for needed ISMS communications.

questions.prompt: Who can help explain the communication arrangements? (Optional)
questions.help: Names and job titles are useful context only. The 2022 source comparison removes the old separate who-shall-communicate item; uncertainty about this optional note does not determine status.

7.5.1.title: Required records
7.5.1.objective: Understand the documented information needed by the standard and by the organization's own ISMS.

questions.prompt: Does the ISMS include the documented information required by the standard?
questions.help: Use the current requirements relevant to this ISMS. The public preview identifies some records, but exact clauses 7–10 still need licensed-text checking; an assumed document checklist is insufficient.
questions.remediation: Include the standard-required documented information in the ISMS.

questions.prompt: Does the ISMS include other documented information the organization needs for effective operation?
questions.help: Consider the complexity of work, people and processes. Existing procedures, pages or records may be enough; no universal policy manual or mandatory document title is introduced.
questions.remediation: Include the documented information needed for effective ISMS operation.

7.5.2.title: Document creation and revision
7.5.2.objective: Understand whether created or revised information is identifiable, usable and appropriately approved.

questions.prompt: Is new or revised documented information appropriately identified?
questions.help: Titles, dates, authors or reference numbers are possible ways to make a record recognizable. They are examples rather than an obligation to use every field.
questions.remediation: Appropriately identify created and revised documented information.

questions.prompt: Is the format appropriate for the documented information's intended use?
questions.help: Consider language, software version or visual presentation as relevant. A word-processing file, managed page or other usable format can work.
questions.remediation: Choose appropriate formats for documented information.

questions.prompt: Is the chosen medium appropriate for the documented information's intended use?
questions.help: Paper and electronic records are alternatives. This does not require changing the organization's established repository or buying a document platform.
questions.remediation: Use appropriate media for documented information.

questions.prompt: Is created or revised documented information reviewed for its suitability and adequacy?
questions.help: Check the organization's actual review approach for the information concerned. The reviewer need not have a prescribed title.
questions.remediation: Review created and revised information for suitability and adequacy.

questions.prompt: Is created or revised documented information appropriately approved?
questions.help: Explain the approval appropriate to the record. Workflow approval, a recorded decision or another controlled method can work; a handwritten signature is not universally required.
questions.remediation: Approve created and revised documented information appropriately.

7.5.3.title: Document protection and availability
7.5.3.objective: Understand availability, protection and lifecycle control of required documented information.

questions.prompt: Can people obtain required documented information where and when they need it?
questions.help: Consider practical retrieval for the intended work. A shared repository, controlled paper records or another suitable arrangement can work.
questions.remediation: Make required documented information available where and when needed.

questions.prompt: Is the information suitable for use when people need it?
questions.help: Consider whether the content and version support the actual task. Being able to find an unusable record is insufficient.
questions.remediation: Keep required documented information suitable for its intended use.

questions.prompt: Is required documented information protected against inappropriate disclosure?
questions.help: Consider the information's confidentiality needs. Access permissions, controlled sharing or physical protections can work according to the information.
questions.remediation: Protect required documented information against inappropriate disclosure.

questions.prompt: Is required documented information protected against improper use?
questions.help: Consider how information can be used only in appropriate ways. The needed safeguards depend on the record and the organization's circumstances.
questions.topic: Document protection and availability: improper use
questions.remediation: Protect required documented information against improper use.

questions.prompt: Is required documented information protected against loss of integrity?
questions.help: Consider unauthorized changes or corruption. Suitable permissions, controlled changes and other equivalent arrangements can support integrity.
questions.remediation: Protect required documented information against loss of integrity.

questions.prompt: Is distribution of documented information controlled as appropriate?
questions.help: Consider how the right information reaches the intended people. Controlled sharing or another suitable distribution arrangement can work.
questions.remediation: Control distribution of documented information as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Is access to documented information controlled as appropriate?
questions.help: Consider who may view or change the information. View and edit permissions can differ; no particular repository product is required.
questions.remediation: Control access to documented information as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Is retrieval of documented information controlled as appropriate?
questions.help: Consider how people locate the correct current information. A managed repository or controlled paper filing can work.
questions.remediation: Control retrieval of documented information as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Is use of documented information controlled as appropriate?
questions.help: Consider whether people rely on appropriate versions and instructions for their work. A particular document-control platform is optional.
questions.remediation: Control use of documented information as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Are storage and preservation arrangements appropriate for documented information?
questions.help: Consider the record's useful life and the risks of damage or loss. This does not prescribe a storage technology or fixed retention duration.
questions.remediation: Store and preserve documented information appropriately.

questions.prompt: Do preservation arrangements keep documented information legible?
questions.help: Consider whether retained information remains readable when needed. A different medium or version arrangement can work if it preserves usability.
questions.remediation: Preserve the legibility of documented information.

questions.prompt: Are changes to documented information controlled as appropriate?
questions.help: Explain how revisions are recognized and superseded instructions handled. Version history or equivalent controls can work.
questions.remediation: Control changes to documented information as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Are retention and disposition of documented information controlled as appropriate?
questions.help: Use actual operational and applicable obligation needs. No fixed number of years or automatic deletion rule is introduced.
questions.remediation: Control retention and disposition of documented information as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Is externally sourced documented information needed for ISMS planning or operation?
questions.help: Consider material such as provider instructions or applicable external requirements. Choose Not relevant here only with a reason; this scopes external-document questions and cannot remove the rest of 7.5.3.
questions.topic: Document protection and availability: external context
questions.remediation: Determine whether necessary externally sourced information is present.

questions.prompt: Is that necessary external information identified appropriately?
questions.help: Use the external material the organization actually relies on. A source reference or controlled link may work; no mandatory external-document register is introduced.
questions.topic: Document protection and availability: external identification
questions.remediation: Identify necessary externally sourced documented information appropriately.

questions.prompt: Is that necessary external information controlled appropriately?
questions.help: Consider access, currency and use within the ISMS. Receiving a supplier file alone does not explain how it is controlled.
questions.topic: Document protection and availability: external control
questions.remediation: Control necessary externally sourced documented information appropriately.

8.1.title: Controlled operational processes
8.1.objective: Understand whether planning is carried into controlled operation, including changes and external provision.

questions.prompt: Have criteria been established for processes needed to meet requirements and implement clause 6 actions?
questions.help: Explain what shows that an operating process has run as intended. Existing procedures or practical criteria can work; a new process manual is optional.
questions.remediation: Establish criteria for the needed operational processes.

questions.prompt: Are those processes implemented and controlled using the established criteria?
questions.help: Trace a planned risk, opportunity or objective action into actual operation. A planned task alone does not demonstrate that the process is controlled.
questions.remediation: Implement and control processes using the established criteria.

questions.prompt: Is documented information available to give the needed confidence that processes ran as planned?
questions.help: The amount and form should suit the process. Suitable execution records or other controlled information may work; no universal evidence-file count is imposed.
questions.remediation: Make sufficient documented information available about operational execution.

questions.prompt: Is there a working approach for controlling planned operational changes?
questions.help: Describe how changes are handled using existing operational processes. This remains relevant even in a period without a change example.
questions.remediation: Arrange control of planned operational changes.

questions.prompt: Were planned changes to relevant operational processes made in this period?
questions.help: If no planned change occurred, choose Not relevant here and explain why. This only scopes the execution example.
questions.remediation: Confirm whether planned operational changes occurred.

questions.prompt: Were those planned changes controlled?
questions.help: Discuss how the organization controlled the actual change. An existing operational change approach can be suitable.
questions.remediation: Control planned changes to relevant operational processes.

questions.prompt: Can the organization review unintended changes and respond to adverse effects when needed?
questions.help: Explain the response approach even if no such change has occurred. No incident-management product or fixed response time is introduced.
questions.remediation: Arrange review of unintended changes and response to adverse effects.

questions.prompt: Did unintended changes affect relevant processes in the period discussed?
questions.help: Choose Not relevant here only if none occurred, and give the reason. Unknown event history should remain Not sure.
questions.remediation: Confirm whether relevant unintended changes occurred.

questions.prompt: Were the consequences of those unintended changes reviewed?
questions.help: Explain what changed and the consequences the organization considered. A ticket's existence alone does not establish review.
questions.remediation: Review the consequences of unintended changes.

questions.prompt: Were adverse effects mitigated where necessary?
questions.help: Describe the response to actual adverse effects. If the review identified no need for mitigation, explain that conclusion rather than inventing a corrective task.
questions.remediation: Mitigate adverse effects of unintended changes where necessary.

groups.title: Externally provided processes, products and services

questions.prompt: Are externally provided processes, products or services relevant to the ISMS?
questions.help: Include hosting, shared services and supplied products where relevant, not only formally outsourced processes. A Not relevant here answer needs a reason and leaves the operational clause present.
questions.remediation: Confirm relevant externally provided processes, products and services.

questions.prompt: Are those relevant external processes, products and services controlled?
questions.help: Explain the organization's actual oversight and controls. Agreements, operating checks or equivalent arrangements can support the answer; a supplier's certification does not automatically settle it.
questions.remediation: Control relevant externally provided processes, products and services.

8.2.title: Risk assessment execution
8.2.objective: Understand scheduled and change-triggered assessments using the established risk criteria.

questions.prompt: Are information security risk assessments carried out at the organization's planned intervals?
questions.help: Use the organization's adopted plan. The public guidance supports planned intervals without prescribing annual or quarterly assessment.
questions.remediation: Carry out risk assessments at the planned intervals.

questions.prompt: Can proposed or occurring significant changes trigger a risk assessment?
questions.help: Explain how changes needing reassessment are recognized. This inquiry remains present even if the period has no significant change; the exact trigger qualifiers await licensed-text comparison.
questions.remediation: Arrange risk assessments for proposed or occurring significant changes.

questions.prompt: Were significant changes proposed or experienced in the period discussed?
questions.help: Consider significant changes affecting in-scope information or dependencies. Not relevant here requires a reason and only scopes the example.
questions.remediation: Confirm whether significant changes relevant to risk assessment occurred or were proposed.

questions.prompt: Were risk assessments performed for those significant changes?
questions.help: Use the actual proposed or occurring changes. Completing the routine assessment does not necessarily show that a separate significant change was considered.
questions.remediation: Assess information security risks arising from significant changes.

questions.prompt: Do the performed assessments use the criteria established under 6.1.2?
questions.help: Compare the operating assessments with the adopted method and criteria. Do not substitute a new scoring method based solely on this interview.
questions.remediation: Use the established risk-assessment criteria.

questions.prompt: Are documented results of the risk assessments retained?
questions.help: Use completed assessments in an appropriate controlled form. A specific risk-register product or export format is not required.
questions.remediation: Retain documented risk-assessment results.

8.3.title: Treatment execution
8.3.objective: Understand whether the treatment plan is implemented and its results retained.

questions.prompt: Is the information security risk-treatment plan being implemented?
questions.help: Trace treatment decisions into actual safeguards or other planned responses. This follows the approved plan; the interview does not prescribe a specific tool or automatically close Actions.
questions.remediation: Implement the information security risk-treatment plan.

questions.prompt: Are documented results of risk treatment retained?
questions.help: Describe what records show the actual treatment results. Plan approval and residual-risk acceptance under 6.1.3 remain separate decisions.
questions.remediation: Retain documented information about risk-treatment results.

9.1.title: Performance measurement
9.1.objective: Understand how valid monitoring and measurement lead to evaluation of security performance and ISMS effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined what needs monitoring and measurement?
questions.help: Consider relevant security processes and controls as well as other performance information. Existing measures can work; a universal metric list is not introduced.
questions.remediation: Determine what needs monitoring and measurement.

questions.prompt: Have suitable monitoring and measurement methods been determined?
questions.help: Explain how the selected methods produce usable information for the actual measure. Manual collection or an existing tool can work.
questions.remediation: Determine suitable monitoring and measurement methods.

questions.prompt: Have suitable methods for analysis and evaluation been determined?
questions.help: Explain how raw results will be interpreted. A dashboard or count alone does not necessarily provide an evaluation method.
questions.remediation: Determine suitable analysis and evaluation methods.

questions.prompt: Do the chosen methods support comparable results?
questions.help: Consider how changes in definitions or populations affect comparison. No particular measurement product is prescribed.
questions.remediation: Resolve method weaknesses that prevent comparable results.

questions.prompt: Do the chosen methods support reproducible results?
questions.help: Consider whether the same method and data can support the same result. This does not require a specific automated test or numeric precision.
questions.remediation: Resolve method weaknesses that prevent reproducible results.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined when monitoring and measurement occur?
questions.help: Use timing appropriate to the measures and the organization's needs. No universal monthly, quarterly or annual interval is imposed.
questions.remediation: Determine timing for monitoring and measurement.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined who performs the monitoring and measurement?
questions.help: Identify the responsibility for this work. A particular role title, dashboard owner field or contact name is not required.
questions.remediation: Determine who performs monitoring and measurement.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined when results are analyzed and evaluated?
questions.help: Collection and analysis may have different timing. The adopted approach should fit the decision being supported.
questions.remediation: Determine when results are analyzed and evaluated.

questions.prompt: Has the organization determined who analyzes and evaluates the results?
questions.help: Explain the assigned evaluation responsibility. Unknown optional contact details do not replace an answer about whether the responsibility is determined.
questions.remediation: Determine who analyzes and evaluates results.

questions.prompt: Is documented information available as evidence of the results?
questions.help: Suitable retained data and evaluation records can work. The interview does not prescribe a separate report title or file count.
questions.remediation: Make documented evidence of monitoring and measurement results available.

questions.prompt: Does the organization evaluate its information security performance?
questions.help: Explain the conclusion drawn from relevant results and information. Merely collecting metrics does not evaluate performance.
questions.remediation: Evaluate information security performance.

questions.prompt: Does the organization evaluate how effective the ISMS is?
questions.help: Discuss whether the management system achieves its intended outcomes. A single control check does not by itself evaluate the whole ISMS.
questions.remediation: Evaluate ISMS effectiveness.

9.2.1.title: ISMS audit coverage
9.2.1.objective: Understand whether internal audits evaluate conformity and effective ISMS operation at planned intervals.

questions.prompt: Are internal audits conducted at the planned intervals?
questions.help: Use the organization's adopted audit plan. Public guidance supports planned intervals; it does not impose a universal annual or quarterly audit.
questions.remediation: Conduct internal audits at planned intervals.

questions.prompt: Do audits provide information about conformity with the organization's own ISMS requirements?
questions.help: Consider the actual adopted rules and processes in the audit scope. A document inventory alone does not evaluate conformity.
questions.remediation: Audit conformity with the organization's own ISMS requirements.

questions.prompt: Do audits provide information about conformity with the standard's requirements?
questions.help: Use legitimate access to the current standard for audit criteria. These interview questions are original readiness guidance and do not establish complete normative audit coverage.
questions.remediation: Audit conformity with ISO/IEC 27001 requirements.

questions.prompt: Do audits evaluate whether the ISMS is effectively implemented?
questions.help: Consider tests of actual operation rather than only checking whether procedures exist. The method should suit the audited activity.
questions.remediation: Evaluate effective implementation of the ISMS in internal audits.

questions.prompt: Do audits evaluate whether the ISMS is effectively maintained?
questions.help: Consider continued operation and upkeep. A past certification or a one-time audit does not answer the current operating question.
questions.remediation: Evaluate effective maintenance of the ISMS in internal audits.

9.2.2.title: Internal audit program
9.2.2.objective: Understand the audit program, each audit's boundaries, impartial conduct, reporting and records.

questions.prompt: Is an internal audit program planned and established?
questions.help: Describe how the organization arranges internal audit activity. A program can use existing review arrangements; a new audit platform is optional.
questions.remediation: Plan and establish the internal audit program.

questions.prompt: Is the audit program implemented?
questions.help: Compare planned activity with what actually occurs. Having a calendar without audit work does not demonstrate implementation.
questions.remediation: Implement the internal audit program.

questions.prompt: Is the audit program maintained?
questions.help: Explain how the program remains workable as coverage and conditions change. No universal revision interval is introduced.
questions.remediation: Maintain the internal audit program.

questions.prompt: Does the program specify its audit frequency?
questions.help: Use planned frequency suited to the organization. A preset quarterly product schedule is not an ISO mandate.
questions.remediation: Specify planned frequency in the audit program.

questions.prompt: Does the program specify the methods used for audits?
questions.help: Interviews, record examination, observation and suitable testing may be combined. A specific checklist tool is optional.
questions.remediation: Specify methods in the audit program.

questions.prompt: Does the program specify audit responsibilities?
questions.help: Identify responsibilities for planning and conducting work. Job titles are flexible; assignment of the duties is substantive.
questions.remediation: Specify responsibilities in the audit program.

questions.prompt: Does the program specify audit planning requirements?
questions.help: Explain what needs to be arranged before an audit. No universal planning template or lead time is prescribed.
questions.remediation: Specify planning requirements in the audit program.

questions.prompt: Does the program specify reporting arrangements?
questions.help: Describe how audit information is recorded and communicated. An existing report or review record can work.
questions.remediation: Specify reporting arrangements in the audit program.

questions.prompt: Does program planning consider the importance of the processes being audited?
questions.help: Explain how important processes affect attention and coverage. This does not impose an identical audit duration for every process.
questions.remediation: Consider process importance when establishing the audit program.

questions.prompt: Does program planning consider previous audit results?
questions.help: Use relevant prior results where they exist. For a first audit, explain that there are no earlier results rather than inventing history.
questions.remediation: Consider previous audit results when establishing the audit program.

groups.title: Criteria and scope of each audit

questions.prompt: Are criteria defined for each audit?
questions.help: Identify the requirements against which the activity will be evaluated. Document presence is not an audit criterion by itself.
questions.remediation: Define criteria for each internal audit.

questions.prompt: Is the scope defined for each audit?
questions.help: Describe the activities, processes or parts covered. Individual audit scope can vary while the program addresses the ISMS.
questions.remediation: Define the scope of each internal audit.

questions.prompt: Do auditor selection and audit conduct support objective conclusions?
questions.help: Discuss suitable skills and how facts are evaluated. Internal or external auditors can be used; a specific certification is not universally required.
questions.remediation: Select auditors and conduct audits supporting objective conclusions.

questions.prompt: Do auditor selection and audit conduct preserve impartiality?
questions.help: Consider conflicts and assessment of one's own work. Suitable arrangements must support impartial evaluation; a vendor's involvement alone does not guarantee it.
questions.remediation: Preserve impartiality in auditor selection and audit conduct.

questions.prompt: Are audit results reported to the relevant management?
questions.help: Explain how results reach the people who need them. Logging a finding without reporting it to relevant management is insufficient.
questions.remediation: Report audit results to relevant management.

questions.prompt: Is documented information available showing implementation of the audit program?
questions.help: Use records demonstrating the actual program work. A particular workbook or audit-management product is optional.
questions.remediation: Make documented evidence of audit-program implementation available.

questions.prompt: Is documented information available showing the audit results?
questions.help: Reports, findings or equivalent controlled records can work. This interview does not automatically close Findings or change audit conclusions.
questions.remediation: Make documented evidence of audit results available.

9.3.1.title: Management review operation
9.3.1.objective: Understand top management's planned review of the ISMS's continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Does top management review the ISMS?
questions.help: Describe management's actual evaluation, which can be supported through appropriate review arrangements. A status meeting without leadership evaluation does not settle this question.
questions.remediation: Ensure top management reviews the ISMS.

questions.prompt: Does that review occur at the planned intervals?
questions.help: Use the organization's adopted review plan. No universal annual, quarterly or monthly interval is imposed.
questions.remediation: Perform management review at planned intervals.

questions.prompt: Does management review whether the ISMS continues to suit the organization?
questions.help: Consider whether the management system still fits actual purpose and circumstances, including relevant context changes.
questions.remediation: Review the ISMS's continuing suitability.

questions.prompt: Does management review whether the ISMS continues to be adequate for its needs?
questions.help: Consider whether the management system is sufficient for relevant requirements and scope. A certification label alone is insufficient.
questions.remediation: Review the ISMS's continuing adequacy.

questions.prompt: Does management review whether the ISMS continues to be effective?
questions.help: Consider actual outcomes and performance information. Completing an agenda alone does not demonstrate management's evaluation.
questions.remediation: Review the ISMS's continuing effectiveness.

9.3.2.title: Management review inputs
9.3.2.objective: Understand whether relevant change, performance, risk and feedback information informs management review.

questions.prompt: Does management review consider the status of actions from earlier management reviews?
questions.help: Use actual decisions and follow-up records. At the first review, explain that there are no prior review actions; do not invent completed actions.
questions.remediation: Bring the status of earlier management-review actions into review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider changes in relevant internal issues?
questions.help: Consider changes in strategy, structure, work or capabilities that affect the ISMS. If no relevant change occurred, explain that assessment.
questions.remediation: Bring relevant internal-context changes into management review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider changes in relevant external issues?
questions.help: Consider actual external conditions and dependencies, including climate effects where relevant. A required input can report no relevant changes.
questions.remediation: Bring relevant external-context changes into management review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider changes in relevant interested-party needs and expectations?
questions.help: Use changes affecting the ISMS, including relevant climate-related requirements. This differs from general stakeholder feedback and remains its own inquiry.
questions.remediation: Bring changes in relevant interested-party needs and expectations into review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider security-performance information and trends in nonconformities?
questions.help: Consider the actual issues and recurring patterns. A no-issue period can still be evaluated; do not require invented findings.
questions.remediation: Bring nonconformity performance information and trends into review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider security-performance information and trends in corrective actions?
questions.help: Consider progress, recurring corrective work and whether actions achieved their purpose. Action closure alone does not explain the performance trend.
questions.topic: Management review inputs: corrective action trends
questions.remediation: Bring corrective-action performance information and trends into review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider monitoring and measurement results and their trends?
questions.help: Use relevant results and explain direction over time where data supports it. Lack of a dashboard product is not itself a gap.
questions.remediation: Bring monitoring and measurement results and trends into review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider audit results and their trends?
questions.help: Use relevant audit conclusions and repeated patterns, rather than only reporting that an audit took place.
questions.remediation: Bring audit results and relevant trends into management review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider fulfillment of security objectives and its trends?
questions.help: Consider actual achievement and progress over time where comparison is meaningful. A list of targets alone does not show fulfillment.
questions.remediation: Bring objective fulfillment and relevant trends into review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider feedback from interested parties?
questions.help: Consider actual relevant feedback, including confirmation that none was received if that is the case. This does not require surveys from every party.
questions.remediation: Bring relevant interested-party feedback into management review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider the results of risk assessment?
questions.help: Use the current assessment information relevant to management's decisions. This does not replace the risk owner's separate approval duties.
questions.remediation: Bring risk-assessment results into management review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider the status of the risk-treatment plan?
questions.help: Consider actual progress and remaining work. A treatment plan's existence does not explain its implementation status.
questions.remediation: Bring risk-treatment plan status into management review.

questions.prompt: Does review consider opportunities for continual improvement?
questions.help: Use meaningful opportunities from the organization's experience. A separate idea register or a new project at every review is optional.
questions.remediation: Bring continual-improvement opportunities into management review.

9.3.3.title: Management review decisions
9.3.3.objective: Understand the recorded decisions about improvement and changes arising from management review.

questions.prompt: Do review results include decisions about continual-improvement opportunities?
questions.help: Describe management's actual conclusion, which may include a reasoned decision not to pursue an opportunity. No new improvement project is required at every review.
questions.remediation: Record management-review decisions about improvement opportunities.

questions.prompt: Do review results include decisions about any need to change the ISMS?
questions.help: Record the decision about needed changes or the conclusion that none are needed. This question is not hidden merely because no change project was approved.
questions.remediation: Record management-review decisions about needed ISMS changes.

questions.prompt: Is documented information available showing the management-review results?
questions.help: Suitable minutes, decision records or an equivalent controlled record can work. A particular meeting title or minute template is optional.
questions.remediation: Make documented evidence of management-review results available.

10.1.title: Ongoing ISMS improvement
10.1.objective: Understand continual improvement in the ISMS's fit, sufficiency and effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Does the organization continually improve how well the ISMS suits its circumstances?
questions.help: Consider changes that make the management system a better fit for actual needs. Existing management review and change processes can support improvement; no dedicated improvement system is required.
questions.remediation: Continually improve ISMS suitability.

questions.prompt: Does the organization continually improve the ISMS's adequacy for its needs?
questions.help: Consider improvements to sufficient coverage or capability for relevant requirements. More documents are not automatically better adequacy.
questions.remediation: Continually improve ISMS adequacy.

questions.prompt: Does the organization continually improve the ISMS's effectiveness?
questions.help: Consider whether changes help the system achieve intended outcomes. Existing performance and review information can support the explanation; a fixed improvement quota is not required.
questions.remediation: Continually improve ISMS effectiveness.

10.2.title: Nonconformity correction
10.2.objective: Understand a working response to nonconformities and the actual correction, cause and effectiveness work when one occurs.

questions.prompt: Is there a working approach for responding when an ISMS nonconformity occurs?
questions.help: Explain how an issue would reach the existing correction and corrective-action process. This remains answerable when no nonconformity occurred; no event-free period makes the whole clause N/A.
questions.remediation: Arrange an appropriate response to ISMS nonconformities.

questions.prompt: Did an ISMS nonconformity occur in the period being discussed?
questions.help: Choose Not relevant here only if no nonconformity occurred, and give the reason. The response-arrangement question remains; this interview cannot certify an event-free period or exclude clause 10.2.
questions.remediation: Confirm whether nonconformity response examples are relevant.

questions.prompt: Was action taken to control and correct the nonconformity as appropriate?
questions.help: Discuss the actual issue and proportionate response. A corrective-action ticket alone does not show containment or correction; not every issue needs the same response.
questions.remediation: Control and correct the nonconformity as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Were the consequences of the nonconformity dealt with?
questions.help: Consider actual effects as well as the immediate defect. If no further consequence needed action, explain that assessment rather than inventing a recovery task.
questions.remediation: Deal with the consequences of the nonconformity.

questions.prompt: Was the nonconformity reviewed to understand what happened?
questions.help: Use actual facts from the affected work. A short review may be sufficient for a simple issue; no root-cause workshop format is imposed.
questions.remediation: Review the nonconformity to understand the issue.

questions.prompt: Were the causes of the nonconformity determined?
questions.help: Consider why the issue happened, rather than only restating the symptom. Different analysis methods can work.
questions.remediation: Determine the causes of the nonconformity.

questions.prompt: Was it determined whether similar nonconformities exist elsewhere?
