questions.help: Consider relevant processes or records beyond the first occurrence. This does not mandate a whole-application audit for every issue.
questions.remediation: Determine whether similar nonconformities exist elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Was it determined whether similar nonconformities could occur elsewhere?
questions.help: Consider where the same cause could create another issue. Avoid assuming that the first corrected record resolves all related exposure.
questions.remediation: Determine whether similar nonconformities could occur elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Was the need for action to eliminate causes and prevent recurrence evaluated?
questions.help: Explain the decision about further action based on the actual cause and potential for recurrence. Immediate correction and evaluation of corrective-action need are separate inquiries.
questions.remediation: Evaluate the need for action against causes and recurrence.

questions.prompt: Was any necessary corrective action implemented?
questions.help: If the cause evaluation found no further action necessary, explain that basis. Otherwise describe the actual changes; creating a plan alone does not implement them.
questions.remediation: Implement necessary corrective action.

questions.prompt: Was corrective action appropriate to the effects of the nonconformity?
questions.help: Discuss a response suited to the actual effects. The same technical solution or approval workflow is not required for every issue.
questions.remediation: Make corrective action appropriate to the effects of the nonconformity.

questions.prompt: Was the effectiveness of any corrective action reviewed?
questions.help: Explain what showed whether the response worked. If no corrective action was needed, state the supported basis. Task completion alone does not establish effectiveness, and this question does not mandate a particular independent reviewer.
questions.remediation: Review the effectiveness of corrective action taken.

questions.prompt: Were changes to the ISMS made if they were necessary?
questions.help: Explain the decision about management-system changes and any resulting work. A reasoned conclusion that no change was needed can be appropriate.
questions.remediation: Make necessary changes to the ISMS following the nonconformity.

questions.prompt: Is documented information available about the nature of the nonconformity?
questions.help: An existing Finding, audit record or another controlled record can describe the issue. No separate nonconformity-register product is required.
questions.remediation: Make documented information about the nonconformity available.

questions.prompt: Is documented information available about the subsequent actions taken?
questions.help: Use actual action history or equivalent records. A planned action without execution does not record an action taken.
questions.remediation: Make documented information about subsequent actions available.

questions.prompt: Is documented information available about the results of corrective action?
questions.help: Record what resulted from the response. If no corrective action was needed, preserve the basis for that conclusion rather than inventing results.
questions.remediation: Make documented information about corrective-action results available.

A.5.1.title: Security policy governance
A.5.1.objective: Understand whether approved security direction is documented, understood and kept suitable for the organization.

questions.prompt: Is the organization's security direction documented in policies suited to its business and protection needs?
questions.help: A concise policy set or controlled sections in existing governance documents can work. Include topic rules where the organization's risks call for them; a prescribed policy title is not needed.
questions.remediation: Document suitable security direction and the topic rules needed to apply it.

questions.prompt: Have the security policies been approved by the appropriate management authority?
questions.help: Explain how approval is established for current versions. An existing document approval route can serve this purpose.
questions.remediation: Obtain appropriate management approval for current security policies.

questions.prompt: Are relevant policies communicated to the people expected to follow them?
questions.help: Use effective communication for employees and relevant external personnel. An intranet, onboarding discussion or contract communication may be appropriate.
questions.remediation: Communicate current policies to their intended audiences.

questions.prompt: Is there a suitable way to establish that those audiences have acknowledged the policies relevant to their work?
questions.help: Signed acknowledgements, recorded induction or another demonstrable approach may work. A subscription or automated attestation product is optional.
questions.remediation: Resolve gaps in establishing acknowledgement of relevant security policies.

questions.prompt: Are policies reviewed at the organization's planned intervals for continued suitability?
questions.help: Use the organization's chosen timing and rationale. This question imposes no annual or quarterly interval.
questions.remediation: Set and carry out suitable policy reviews.

questions.prompt: Are policies reconsidered when significant changes affect their suitability?
questions.help: Consider changed business activities, obligations, threats or technology. A scheduled review alone may miss a material change.
questions.remediation: Reassess affected policies when significant changes arise.

A.5.2.title: Security role allocation
A.5.2.objective: Understand whether security responsibilities are assigned and communicated without gaps in accountability.

questions.prompt: Are responsibilities for important security activities and decisions explicitly assigned?
questions.help: Existing role descriptions, service ownership records or responsibility assignments may suffice. A special security job title is optional.
questions.remediation: Assign responsibility for security activities and decisions that lack an accountable role.

questions.prompt: Do the assigned people understand the security responsibilities they are expected to carry out?
questions.help: Ask about actual duties and decision authority. A person's job title or presence in a contact list is not evidence that duties were communicated.
questions.remediation: Communicate security duties and decision authority to the assigned people.

questions.prompt: Which role coordinates these responsibilities? (Optional)
questions.help: Describe a role if useful; uncertainty about its name alone must not change the implementation result.

questions.prompt: When security work is delegated or supplied externally, is accountability retained and the handoff understood?
questions.help: Delegation can be sensible. Explain who retains the decision responsibility and who performs the work; outsourcing does not remove this inquiry.
questions.remediation: Clarify retained accountability and delegated security work.

A.5.3.title: Separation of conflicting duties
A.5.3.objective: Understand how incompatible duties are identified and constrained to reduce undetected misuse.

questions.prompt: Have duties that could enable misuse without an effective check been identified?
questions.help: Consider sensitive approvals, access administration, payment or production changes where relevant. Start with real process risks rather than a universal role template.
questions.remediation: Identify incompatible duties in sensitive processes.

questions.prompt: Are identified conflicting duties controlled through actual separation, or a justified alternative with evaluated, effective compensating checks?
questions.help: Separate people, approval steps or access privileges can support the outcome. Where that is impractical, describe the evaluated checks that address the conflict, not merely an accepted exception. A reported alternative is not an approval or ISO conformity conclusion.
questions.remediation: Separate conflicting responsibilities and permissions, or evaluate and implement justified, effective checks for the remaining conflicts.

questions.prompt: Where full separation is impractical, are the remaining conflicts explicitly assessed and supported by an effective compensating check?
questions.help: Independent review, transaction oversight or other checks may reduce risk. Their existence does not automatically establish ISO conformity or justify an exception.
questions.remediation: Assess unresolved duty conflicts and establish justified, effective checks.

A.5.4.title: Management security expectations
A.5.4.objective: Understand whether managers require and support security practices in the work they supervise.

questions.prompt: Do managers make the security rules relevant to their teams' work clear?
questions.help: Discuss what people are expected to do before taking on relevant access or tasks. Existing onboarding and team communication can serve this purpose.
questions.remediation: Clarify management expectations for security behavior in each affected team.

questions.prompt: Do managers enable people to apply those rules in their day-to-day work?
questions.help: Consider access to instructions, relevant learning and support when a security concern conflicts with a delivery request. No named management committee is assumed.
questions.remediation: Resolve management or practical barriers to following security rules.

questions.prompt: Do managers follow up when team practices depart from security expectations?
questions.help: Use an actual example if available, otherwise explain the response process. The absence of reported violations does not demonstrate enforcement.
questions.remediation: Establish consistent management follow-through on security departures.

A.5.5.title: Authority liaison
A.5.5.objective: Understand whether relevant authority contacts and the circumstances for using them are known and maintained.

questions.prompt: Are the authorities relevant to security matters in this scope identified with usable contact routes?
questions.help: Consider regulators, law enforcement, emergency services or competent public bodies as relevant. No universal list of agencies applies.
questions.remediation: Identify relevant authorities and usable contact routes.

questions.prompt: Is responsibility for contacting those authorities assigned?
questions.help: Assign a role with authority to coordinate the contact. A dedicated liaison position is optional.
questions.remediation: Assign responsibility for authority liaison.

questions.prompt: Are the circumstances for contacting relevant authorities understood?
questions.help: Use applicable obligations and assessed incident scenarios. Legal advice may be necessary; this interview does not decide whether a notification law applies.
questions.remediation: Clarify applicable triggers and the route for authority contact.

questions.prompt: Are authority contacts maintained so they can be used when needed?
questions.help: Check how changed contacts are noticed and updated. A test call to an emergency number is not required.
questions.remediation: Keep relevant authority contact routes current and accessible.

A.5.6.title: Security community liaison
A.5.6.objective: Understand whether relevant professional communities provide usable security information and support.

questions.prompt: Are contacts with useful security communities or professional groups established?
questions.help: A sector information-sharing group, professional forum, public advisory community or equivalent contact can work. Paid membership is optional.
questions.remediation: Establish suitable security community or professional contacts.

questions.prompt: Can relevant information or assistance be obtained through those contacts?
questions.help: Describe how updates, peer knowledge or specialist help reach someone able to consider them. Membership alone is not the intended outcome.
questions.remediation: Make professional contacts usable for relevant information and assistance.

questions.prompt: Are these contacts maintained so they remain relevant and usable?
questions.help: Use an approach proportionate to the organization; there is no prescribed meeting or subscription schedule.
questions.remediation: Maintain useful security community contact routes.

A.5.7.title: Threat-informed decisions
A.5.7.objective: Understand whether threat information is collected, analyzed and used to support protective decisions.

questions.prompt: Is threat information relevant to the organization's information and services obtained?
questions.help: Public advisories, provider alerts, sector sharing and internal observations may work. A commercial threat intelligence platform is optional.
questions.remediation: Obtain threat information suited to the organization's exposure.

questions.prompt: Which sources or tools are used? (Optional)
questions.help: Names provide context only. Not knowing a tool or supplier name must not decide implementation.

questions.prompt: Is collected information analyzed for what it means to the organization's exposure?
questions.help: Explain how relevance, credibility and likely impact are considered. Simply forwarding every alert is not analysis.
questions.remediation: Analyze threat information for organizational relevance.

questions.prompt: Does relevant threat analysis reach the people who can act on it?
questions.help: Existing operational meetings, alerts or risk discussions can be sufficient. Use the audience appropriate to the information.
questions.remediation: Route relevant threat analysis to appropriate decision makers.

questions.prompt: Does that analysis inform security or risk decisions?
questions.help: Action, a justified no-action decision or a revised risk assessment can demonstrate use. A threat report alone does not.
questions.remediation: Connect threat analysis to reasoned protective decisions.

A.5.8.title: Security in projects
A.5.8.objective: Understand whether project security needs influence decisions and remain considered through delivery.

questions.prompt: Are security needs identified while a project's key decisions can still be influenced?
questions.help: Include relevant non-IT projects as well as technical projects. Existing planning or acceptance requirements may hold the information.
questions.remediation: Identify relevant security needs early enough to influence project decisions.

questions.prompt: Are security risks associated with the project assessed and assigned for treatment?
questions.help: Consider risks to information and services created or changed by the project. Reuse the organization's risk process rather than creating a separate mandatory register.
questions.remediation: Assess project security risks and assign treatment responsibility.

questions.prompt: Are security requirements and decisions followed through as the project develops?
questions.help: Use proportionate review points or change discussions. A specific stage-gate method is optional.
questions.remediation: Track security decisions through project delivery.

questions.prompt: Are unresolved security issues considered before the project's results are accepted?
questions.help: Acceptance may involve remediation or authorized risk decisions. A signed checklist alone does not show issues were considered.
questions.remediation: Resolve or explicitly decide outstanding security issues before acceptance.

A.5.9.title: Asset and information inventory
A.5.9.objective: Understand whether information and supporting assets are known, assigned owners and kept represented in the inventory.

questions.prompt: Does the inventory cover the information and associated assets relevant to this scope?
questions.help: Include data, systems, services and other relevant assets, including assets operated by a provider. Existing inventories can be linked rather than duplicated.
questions.remediation: Close gaps in the inventory of relevant information and associated assets.

questions.prompt: Are accountable owners identified for the inventoried information and assets?
questions.help: Ownership may be assigned to a role. Custody by a provider does not eliminate internal accountability for the supported business activity.
questions.remediation: Assign accountable ownership for relevant information and assets.

questions.prompt: Is the inventory maintained as information and assets are introduced, changed or retired?
questions.help: Manual reconciliation, discovery tools or owner updates can work. No fixed discovery interval is imposed.
questions.remediation: Maintain inventory accuracy as assets and information change.

A.5.10.title: Acceptable-use rules
A.5.10.objective: Understand whether acceptable use and handling boundaries are documented and understood by affected users.

questions.prompt: Are acceptable uses of information and associated assets documented?
questions.help: A policy, employment guidance or controlled instructions can work. Use clear business boundaries rather than requiring a document called Acceptable Use Policy.
questions.remediation: Document appropriate acceptable-use boundaries.

questions.prompt: Are handling procedures available for the information and assets people use?
questions.help: Explain safe storage, sharing or other handling relevant to the activity. Topic-specific existing procedures can serve this purpose.
questions.remediation: Establish usable handling procedures for relevant information and assets.

questions.prompt: Do affected users understand the use and handling rules relevant to them?
questions.help: Include relevant external users. Communication and a practical explanation can demonstrate understanding; a particular attestation tool is optional.
questions.remediation: Communicate relevant use and handling rules to affected users.

A.5.11.title: Asset return
A.5.11.objective: Understand whether assets entrusted to people or other parties are recovered when the relationship or need changes.

questions.prompt: Can assets held by people or other parties be identified when return is due?
questions.help: Consider equipment, media, documents and other entrusted assets. A custody record or linked inventory may be sufficient.
questions.remediation: Identify entrusted assets and the relationships responsible for them.

questions.prompt: Are asset-return responsibilities and triggers established for departures or relationship changes?
questions.help: Include employees, contractors and suppliers holding assets. Existing exit or contract processes can work; outsourcing is not an exclusion.
questions.remediation: Define return responsibilities and triggers for relevant relationship changes.

questions.prompt: Is required asset return followed through until items are recovered or an authorized resolution is recorded?
questions.help: If no departure has occurred, describe the established process. A write-off or unresolved item must be explicit rather than recorded as successful return.
questions.remediation: Follow up outstanding assets and document authorized resolution.

A.5.12.title: Information classification
A.5.12.objective: Understand whether classifications reflect information protection needs and guide its treatment.

questions.prompt: Does the classification approach distinguish information according to its protection needs?
questions.help: Consider confidentiality, integrity, availability, business impact and applicable commitments. Existing impact or sensitivity categories can work if meaningful.
questions.remediation: Define classification criteria suited to information protection needs.

questions.prompt: Are classifications assigned to relevant information using those criteria?
questions.help: Owners may classify data sets, records or categories rather than every individual file. Classification should reflect actual use and consequences.
questions.remediation: Apply suitable classifications to relevant information.

questions.prompt: Are classifications understood consistently enough to guide information handling?
questions.help: Map different provider or customer schemes where needed. The same words can mean different protection levels across organizations.
questions.remediation: Clarify classification meanings and associated handling expectations.

questions.prompt: Are classifications reconsidered when the information's protection needs change?
questions.help: Consider changed purpose, audience or obligations. This is an operational review prompt, not a fixed review frequency.
questions.remediation: Reassess classifications when protection needs change.

A.5.13.title: Classification labels
A.5.13.objective: Understand whether information labels reliably communicate the chosen classification scheme.

questions.prompt: Are labelling procedures defined for information formats used in this scope?
questions.help: A visible marking, metadata, container label or other recognizable indicator may work. Explain justified exceptions where a label is impractical.
questions.remediation: Define suitable labelling procedures and justified exceptions.

questions.prompt: Do applied labels correspond to the information's classification?
questions.help: Inspect representative documents, messages or records as appropriate. Avoid exposing sensitive information merely to demonstrate a label.
questions.remediation: Correct labelling that does not reflect the classification scheme.

questions.prompt: Can people or systems using the information interpret its labels correctly?
questions.help: Use a consistent meaning for the selected format. Automated enforcement is optional; labels should support the intended handling.
questions.remediation: Make labels recognizable and their meaning clear to recipients.

A.5.14.title: Protected information transfers
A.5.14.objective: Understand whether transfer rules and protections cover relevant internal and external information movements.

questions.prompt: Are rules and procedures established for the ways information is transferred in this scope?
questions.help: Consider electronic transfers, physical media or paper, and verbal exchange where used. Existing procedures can cover several methods without a new policy for each.
questions.remediation: Define transfer rules and procedures for the methods actually used.

questions.prompt: Are transferred information and intended recipients protected in line with the information's needs?
questions.help: Recipient checks, suitable channels and safeguards against loss or alteration can work. Encryption is one option for relevant channels, not a universal answer to every transfer.
questions.remediation: Apply suitable transfer protections and recipient checks.

questions.prompt: Do information transfers with outside parties occur in this scope?
questions.help: Include transfers through providers acting for the organization. Not relevant here applies only to the following external-transfer inquiry and requires a reason; internal transfer questions remain active.

questions.prompt: Are responsibilities and appropriate protections agreed with the outside parties receiving or sending information?
questions.help: Contract terms, exchange agreements or equivalent agreed arrangements can work. Cover the actual transfer relationship rather than assuming the provider handles every responsibility.
questions.remediation: Agree appropriate transfer responsibilities and protections with outside parties.

A.5.15.title: Access rules
A.5.15.objective: Understand whether physical and logical access decisions follow clear business and protection rules.

questions.prompt: Are access rules established from business needs and information protection requirements?
questions.help: Include relevant physical and logical access. A shared policy or role rules can work; the inquiry is about decision criteria rather than a named document.
questions.remediation: Define access rules suited to business need and protection requirements.

questions.prompt: Are access decisions and enforcement consistent with those rules?
questions.help: Consider permissions as granted in systems and access to places or records. A written policy without effective restrictions is insufficient.
questions.remediation: Apply access rules in authorization and enforcement.

questions.prompt: Do the rules constrain access that is unnecessary for the person's or service's role?
questions.help: Use appropriate least-privilege or need-to-know restrictions. Emergency access can have justified conditions; a broad default entitlement needs examination.
questions.remediation: Restrict unnecessary access and define justified exceptions.

A.5.16.title: Identity lifecycle
A.5.16.objective: Understand whether identities are established, changed and retired with appropriate accountability.

questions.prompt: Is identity creation controlled so the identity represents an authorized person or service?
questions.help: Use a suitable verification and approval route. Existing HR, service ownership or identity provider processes can work; no product is prescribed.
questions.remediation: Establish authorized identity creation and appropriate verification.

questions.prompt: Can an identity's use be connected to the responsible person or service?
questions.help: Individual identities are useful for accountability. Where shared or non-human identities are necessary, explain retained responsibility and justified restrictions rather than assuming they are forbidden.
questions.remediation: Resolve identities that lack accountable ownership or traceability.

questions.prompt: Are identities kept accurate when the person's or service's relationship changes?
questions.help: Include contractors, providers and non-human identities where relevant. Consider name, affiliation and ownership changes; permission decisions remain separately assessed.
questions.remediation: Maintain accurate identities as relationships and responsibilities change.

questions.prompt: Are identities retired or disabled when their authorized purpose ends?
questions.help: Explain how orphaned or duplicate identities are noticed and resolved. Provider management does not remove responsibility to arrange appropriate retirement.
questions.remediation: Retire unneeded identities and resolve orphaned identity records.

A.5.17.title: Credential handling
A.5.17.objective: Understand whether authentication information is issued, handled and changed through controlled processes.

questions.prompt: Is the recipient verified before authentication information is issued or reset?
questions.help: Use established identity verification for initial issuance and recovery. An unverified request alone is insufficient.
questions.remediation: Verify recipients and protect issuance or reset of authentication information.

questions.prompt: Is authentication information delivered or made available through an appropriately protected route?
questions.help: Use secure provisioning suited to the authenticator and recipient. A secure reset decision can still be undermined by exposed delivery.
questions.remediation: Protect delivery of authentication information.

questions.prompt: Is authentication information protected against unauthorized disclosure or use while held or handled?
questions.help: Consider passwords, keys, tokens and recovery material as relevant. Approved secret storage or managed authenticators can work; do not enter secrets into this interview.
questions.remediation: Protect authentication information during storage and handling.

questions.prompt: Are users and administrators told how to handle their authentication information safely?
questions.help: Explain relevant non-sharing, reporting and recovery instructions for the methods actually used. A password manager product is optional.
questions.remediation: Provide appropriate advice for handling authentication information.

questions.prompt: Can exposed, lost or no-longer-authorized authentication information be changed or revoked through the established process?
questions.help: Use the relevant trigger for the authenticator. This question does not impose periodic password rotation or a single rule for all authentication methods.
questions.remediation: Establish change or revocation for compromised or no-longer-authorized authenticators.

A.5.18.title: Access entitlement lifecycle
A.5.18.objective: Understand whether permissions are granted, reviewed, changed and removed according to authorized need.

questions.prompt: Are permissions approved by an appropriate authority before access is provided?
questions.help: Apply the access rules to people and services. Existing role or request approvals can work if responsibility is clear.
questions.remediation: Require suitable approval before providing access rights.

questions.prompt: Are existing access rights reviewed against current business need?
questions.help: Use suitable planned or triggered reviews and decision-quality information. A reviewer confirming an unexplained list is weak support; no annual or quarterly interval is imposed.
questions.remediation: Review access rights against current need and act on inappropriate rights.

questions.prompt: Are access rights adjusted when duties or authorized needs change?
questions.help: Include transfers, provider changes and service ownership changes. Updating identity attributes alone may leave old permissions intact.
questions.remediation: Adjust permissions when authorized needs change.

questions.prompt: Are access rights removed when they are no longer authorized?
questions.help: Include relationship endings and temporary access expiry. Explain how relevant systems and external services are covered.
questions.remediation: Remove unneeded rights across relevant access paths.

A.5.19.title: Supplier security
A.5.19.objective: Understand whether supplier-related security risks are identified and managed with retained organizational accountability.

questions.prompt: Are supplier relationships that can affect information security identified?
questions.help: Include services, products, subcontracted activities and providers with information or access. Outsourcing an activity creates a relationship to assess, not an automatic exclusion.
questions.remediation: Identify suppliers that can affect information security.

questions.prompt: Is the security exposure of those relationships assessed before reliance on the supplier?
questions.help: Assess access, information, criticality and dependency as appropriate. Questionnaires, discussions or independent assurance can inform the assessment; a required vendor score is not imposed.
questions.remediation: Assess relevant supplier security exposure.

questions.prompt: Are processes established to address the supplier security risks identified?
questions.help: Use proportionate selection, onboarding and operating controls. Existing procurement and vendor processes can support this; no parallel supplier register is needed.
questions.remediation: Establish supplier processes that address identified security risks.

questions.prompt: Are internal and supplier responsibilities for those protections understood?
questions.help: Know what remains the customer's responsibility and how provider assurance is considered. A supplier certification does not settle every responsibility.
questions.remediation: Clarify retained and supplier security responsibilities.

A.5.20.title: Contractual supplier safeguards
A.5.20.objective: Understand whether supplier agreements capture suitable security responsibilities for the actual relationship.

questions.prompt: Are the security requirements for each relevant supplier relationship identified before agreement?
questions.help: Use the information, access and service dependency at stake. A standard template can help but may need adjustment for the relationship.
questions.remediation: Identify relationship-specific security requirements.

questions.prompt: Are suitable security requirements agreed and recorded with the supplier?
questions.help: A contract, service terms or another demonstrable agreement may work. Review actual commitments rather than relying solely on a marketing statement or questionnaire.
questions.remediation: Agree and record appropriate supplier security commitments.

questions.prompt: Do agreed arrangements clarify how incidents requiring both parties' action will be coordinated?
questions.help: Consider relevant incident notices and assistance. The timing follows applicable agreements or obligations; no arbitrary hours-to-notify rule is introduced.
questions.remediation: Clarify agreed coordination for relevant security issues.

questions.prompt: Do agreed arrangements address material supplier changes that could affect security?
questions.help: Identify appropriate notice and review responsibilities for relevant service or relationship changes. A specific notice period is not imposed.
questions.remediation: Agree appropriate responsibilities for material supplier security changes.

questions.prompt: Do agreements address security responsibilities when the relationship or service ends?
questions.help: Consider appropriate access removal, information return or deletion, and continuing confidentiality duties. Terms should match what the supplier actually holds or provides.
questions.remediation: Agree suitable security responsibilities for ending the supplier relationship.

A.5.21.title: Technology supply-chain safeguards
A.5.21.objective: Understand whether security risks in technology products and services are considered beyond the direct supplier.

questions.prompt: Are important technology supply-chain dependencies recognized when products or services are obtained?
questions.help: Consider relevant components, upstream service providers and supplier reliance. Provider-operated technology remains a dependency even if procurement is outsourced.
questions.remediation: Identify material technology supply-chain dependencies.

questions.prompt: Are security risks from those dependencies assessed?
questions.help: Consider inappropriate changes, counterfeit or compromised components, service interruption or other relevant scenarios. This is a practical risk inquiry, not a mandatory universal test suite.
questions.remediation: Assess material security risks from technology supply-chain dependencies.

questions.prompt: Are appropriate security expectations carried through the relevant technology supply chain?
questions.help: Supplier obligations, assurance, accepted-source restrictions or other controls can work. A software bill of materials may help in a relevant setting but is not universally required.
questions.remediation: Establish appropriate controls and supplier expectations for chain risks.

questions.prompt: Are material supply-chain changes considered for their effect on the selected protections?
questions.help: Use change notifications, review or another proportionate route. Consider provider subcontracting and changed components where relevant.
questions.remediation: Reassess protections when material supply-chain dependencies change.

A.5.22.title: Supplier service oversight
A.5.22.objective: Understand whether supplier service security is monitored, reviewed and protected during changes.

questions.prompt: Is relevant supplier security performance monitored against the agreed expectations?
questions.help: Use service information, incident reports or appropriate assurance evidence. Outsourced monitoring still requires a usable route to the organization.
questions.remediation: Monitor supplier delivery against relevant security expectations.

questions.prompt: Are supplier review results considered and identified security gaps followed up?
questions.help: Independent reports, direct review or other suitable assurance can work. Consider scope and exceptions rather than treating a certificate as a complete answer.
questions.remediation: Assess supplier assurance results and follow up material gaps.

questions.prompt: Are supplier service changes assessed and managed when they may affect security?
questions.help: Consider scope, hosting, subcontractors, interfaces or support arrangements as relevant. A signed agreement does not ensure later changes are controlled.
questions.remediation: Assess and manage security effects of material supplier changes.

A.5.23.title: Cloud service governance
A.5.23.objective: Understand how cloud acquisition, use, management and exit are governed, including customer-side responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Are processes established to govern cloud acquisition, use, management and exit in line with security needs?
questions.help: Explain how proposed cloud use is considered even if no service is currently used. Existing supplier processes can cover cloud-specific needs. This question remains active regardless of the following branch.
questions.remediation: Establish suitable processes for the cloud lifecycle.

questions.prompt: Are cloud services used or being acquired for activities in this scope?
questions.help: Include SaaS and provider-managed cloud supporting the activity. Outsourcing is not a reason to select Not relevant here. That choice needs a reason and hides only service-specific follow-up.

questions.prompt: Are the security needs and provider capabilities assessed for the cloud services used or being acquired?
questions.help: Consider data, service dependency and relevant obligations. Appropriate service review or assurance may work without a dedicated cloud procurement product.
questions.remediation: Assess cloud security needs and provider capability before reliance.

questions.prompt: Are provider and customer security responsibilities understood for those cloud services?
questions.help: Identify customer-managed accounts, configuration and data duties where relevant. A managed service does not transfer every responsibility.
questions.remediation: Clarify provider and retained customer security responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Are retained cloud security responsibilities actually managed during use and material changes?
questions.help: Consider applicable configuration, access and service assurance work. Use the controls suited to the service model rather than assuming identical duties for SaaS and infrastructure.
questions.remediation: Carry out retained cloud security duties and reassess material changes.

questions.prompt: Are workable security arrangements established for exiting those cloud services?
questions.help: Consider information retrieval, access ending, deletion commitments and continuity as relevant. An exit plan may use existing supplier procedures; do not assume provider backups disappear instantly.
questions.remediation: Establish suitable security arrangements for cloud exit.

A.5.24.title: Incident preparation
A.5.24.objective: Understand whether incident roles, procedures and support are ready for use.

questions.prompt: Are incident response responsibilities and decision authority defined and communicated?
questions.help: Include coordination with contracted responders where used. An external response service does not eliminate internal decisions.
questions.remediation: Assign and communicate incident responsibilities and decision authority.

questions.prompt: Are procedures established for recognizing, escalating and handling incidents?
questions.help: Existing response instructions can work. Keep stages usable for the organization rather than requiring a particular plan title.
questions.remediation: Establish usable incident handling procedures.

questions.prompt: Can responders obtain the information and resources they need when an incident occurs?
questions.help: Consider contacts, skills, available assistance and access to procedures when normal systems are affected. Exercises can demonstrate readiness; no prescribed exercise frequency is asserted.
questions.remediation: Resolve barriers to obtaining response information and resources.

questions.prompt: Could an incident require coordination with a supplier, customer, authority or other outside party?
questions.help: Consider shared services and applicable notification obligations. Lack of a previous incident does not make coordination irrelevant. Not relevant here requires a reason and affects only the next inquiry.

questions.prompt: Are appropriate incident contact routes and coordination responsibilities established with those parties?
questions.help: Use existing agreement contacts and applicable obligations. Determine notification duties from facts and advice; a universal reporting deadline is not imposed.
questions.remediation: Prepare contact routes and responsibilities for relevant outside-party incident coordination.

A.5.25.title: Event triage
A.5.25.objective: Understand whether security events are assessed and classified for an appropriate response.

questions.prompt: Are criteria established to decide when a security event should be treated as an incident?
questions.help: Severity categories, response thresholds or another clear decision approach can work. The absence of past incidents does not remove the need for triage readiness.
questions.remediation: Define criteria for assessing events and declaring incidents.

questions.prompt: Can reported security events reach a responsible person for assessment?
questions.help: Consider how reports from people, systems or providers are routed. The route should support timely judgment appropriate to the event.
questions.remediation: Route reported security events to responsible assessors.

questions.prompt: Are event decisions recorded and escalated in line with the assessment?
questions.help: Use a case record, report or other appropriate trace. If no event has occurred, explain the prepared process without claiming tested historical effectiveness.
questions.remediation: Record event decisions and escalate incidents according to the assessment.

A.5.26.title: Incident response execution
A.5.26.objective: Understand whether incident response procedures support coordinated action and are applied to actual incidents when present.

questions.prompt: Is a coordinated response process available for identified incidents?
questions.help: Explain how containment, investigation, recovery or other appropriate actions are coordinated. Existing procedures can fit the incident type; a particular response product is optional.
questions.remediation: Establish a coordinated process for responding to identified incidents.

questions.prompt: Are responsibilities and authorization for consequential response actions clear?
questions.help: Consider actions that could interrupt service, affect evidence or involve third parties. Outsourced responders still need understood authority and retained accountability.
questions.remediation: Clarify authority for consequential incident response actions.

questions.prompt: Have identified incidents requiring response occurred in the period being discussed?
questions.help: No incidents can legitimately mean this historical branch is not relevant; give a reason. Prepared response and decision questions remain active. Exercises provide separate readiness evidence.

questions.prompt: Were those incidents handled using the appropriate response procedures?
questions.help: Describe a redacted example and material departures from the procedure. A plan alone does not prove response was executed.
questions.remediation: Apply response procedures to actual incidents and address material departures.

questions.prompt: Were significant response decisions and actions retained in a usable record?
questions.help: A case timeline or equivalent record can work. Minimize personal or sensitive incident detail in this interview.
questions.remediation: Retain usable records of material incident response decisions and actions.

A.5.27.title: Incident lessons
A.5.27.objective: Understand how incident experience is converted into improvements without assuming incidents have occurred.

questions.prompt: Is there an established way to extract useful lessons from security incidents?
questions.help: Existing incident review or improvement processes can work. If no incidents have occurred, describe the method; exercises can inform readiness but are not represented as actual incidents.
questions.remediation: Establish a method for learning from security incidents.

questions.prompt: Is actual incident experience available to review in the period being discussed?
questions.help: Include incidents in relevant outsourced activities when information is available. Not relevant here needs a reason and hides only the historical learning questions.

questions.prompt: Was available incident experience analyzed for lessons about weaknesses in security arrangements?
questions.help: Consider how the incident arose and what helped or hindered handling. A formal root-cause technique is optional.
questions.remediation: Analyze available incident experience for meaningful lessons.

questions.prompt: Were useful lessons applied to strengthen relevant security arrangements?
questions.help: An adjusted control, procedure or learning activity can work. Recording lessons without a decision or follow-through is weak support.
questions.remediation: Apply useful incident lessons to relevant security arrangements.

A.5.28.title: Incident evidence preservation
A.5.28.objective: Understand whether potential incident evidence can be collected and protected for its intended use.

questions.prompt: Are procedures established to identify and collect potential incident evidence appropriately?
questions.help: Consider records, media and other relevant artifacts. Use suitable specialist or legal advice where needed; a forensic laboratory or specific tool is not universally required.
questions.remediation: Establish appropriate procedures for identifying and collecting potential evidence.

questions.prompt: Do those procedures protect potential evidence against loss or unauthorized alteration?
questions.help: Original preservation, appropriate copies and restricted handling may help. Select methods suited to the artifact and intended use rather than asserting universal legal admissibility.
questions.remediation: Protect potential evidence integrity and handling traceability.

questions.prompt: Do evidence-handling procedures retain the artifact's origin and handling history?
questions.help: Provenance records and custody logs or equivalent traceability can work. Suitable method depends on intended investigative or legal use.
questions.remediation: Retain appropriate evidence provenance and handling history.

questions.prompt: Can evidence handling be performed by people with suitable competence and authority?
questions.help: Internal capability or qualified assistance can work. The organization's responsibility to arrange suitable handling remains when investigation is outsourced.
questions.remediation: Arrange competent and authorized handling of potential evidence.

questions.prompt: Has potential incident evidence been handled in cases relevant to this discussion?
questions.help: Not relevant here requires a reason and affects only the historical inquiry. No incident history does not hide evidence preparation questions.

questions.prompt: Was potential evidence handled in accordance with the established procedures?
questions.help: Use a redacted case or handling record where available. Do not upload sensitive incident artifacts merely to answer this interview.
questions.remediation: Address departures from established evidence handling in actual cases.

A.5.29.title: Security during disruptions
A.5.29.objective: Understand whether appropriate security is planned and maintained while normal operations are disrupted.

questions.prompt: Have the security needs of disrupted or degraded operations been determined?
questions.help: Consider alternate work, emergency access and temporary information handling appropriate to the scope. Use continuity and risk decisions already made.
questions.remediation: Determine security needs for disrupted or degraded operations.

questions.prompt: Are arrangements established to maintain an appropriate level of security during disruption?
questions.help: Alternative safeguards can be appropriate when a normal safeguard is unavailable. Decisions should be assessed; emergency work is not automatic permission to remove protections.
questions.remediation: Establish suitable security safeguards for degraded operations.

questions.prompt: Have the arrangements been checked for practical usability?
questions.help: A scenario review, exercise or representative evaluation can help. This guidance inquiry does not impose a fixed exercise calendar.
questions.remediation: Evaluate whether disruption safeguards can be used in practice.

questions.prompt: Has a disruption requiring these arrangements occurred in the period being discussed?
questions.help: Not relevant here needs a reason and hides only the historical inquiry. Prepared security arrangements remain part of the discussion.

questions.prompt: Were appropriate security safeguards maintained during that disruption?
questions.help: Discuss relevant temporary changes and subsequent restoration. A continuity plan alone does not show what happened during a disruption.
questions.remediation: Address security weaknesses observed during disrupted operations.

A.5.30.title: ICT continuity preparedness
A.5.30.objective: Understand whether ICT recovery capability supports the organization's continuity objectives.

questions.prompt: Are ICT continuity requirements determined from the organization's business continuity needs?
questions.help: Business impact analysis or an equivalent evaluated approach can identify critical services and recovery needs. Do not invent recovery times or data-loss tolerances.
questions.remediation: Determine ICT continuity requirements from business needs.

questions.prompt: Are ICT continuity arrangements implemented to support those requirements?
questions.help: Include dependencies on providers, facilities, connectivity and data where relevant. A backup alone may not provide a complete recovery capability.
questions.remediation: Implement ICT arrangements suited to the continuity requirements.

questions.prompt: Are ICT continuity arrangements maintained as services and dependencies change?
questions.help: Use existing change and service processes. A provider-operated recovery capability still needs appropriate internal coordination.
questions.remediation: Keep ICT recovery arrangements aligned with changed services and dependencies.

questions.prompt: Are ICT continuity arrangements tested against the relevant recovery requirements?
questions.help: Use representative testing suited to risk, safety and dependency. No annual interval or required disruptive production test is introduced.
questions.remediation: Test ICT recovery capability against relevant continuity requirements.

questions.prompt: Are material shortcomings revealed by continuity testing addressed?
questions.help: Track capability gaps and resulting decisions through existing improvement work. A successful isolated restore does not automatically establish every service's recovery capability.
questions.remediation: Resolve material shortcomings in tested recovery capability.

A.5.31.title: Applicable obligations
A.5.31.objective: Understand whether information security obligations are identified, kept current and connected to operating practices.

questions.prompt: Are legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual information security obligations relevant to this scope identified?
questions.help: Use appropriate expertise for the jurisdictions, activities and commitments involved. This interview does not determine legal applicability from answers or prescribe a universal law list.
questions.remediation: Identify applicable information security obligations with appropriate expertise.

questions.prompt: Are relevant obligations recorded in a form people can use to guide security decisions?
questions.help: A register, contract inventory or linked process documentation can work. Avoid storing unnecessary legal or personal detail in the interview.
questions.remediation: Record relevant obligations in a usable form.

questions.prompt: Are appropriate security measures and responsibilities established to meet identified obligations?
questions.help: Trace an obligation to an actual process or safeguard. Listing a law does not demonstrate the required response was implemented.
questions.remediation: Assign and implement suitable responses to identified security obligations.

questions.prompt: Are changed obligations identified and considered for their effect on security arrangements?
questions.help: Use relevant legal, regulatory and contract review channels. No universal subscription or review interval is required.
questions.remediation: Maintain obligation information and update affected security arrangements.

A.5.32.title: Intellectual-property safeguards
A.5.32.objective: Understand whether procedures protect intellectual property and respect rights in material used by the organization.

questions.prompt: Are procedures established to protect intellectual property rights relevant to the organization's information and materials?
questions.help: Consider information created by the organization and rights in software, documentation or other content. Existing procurement and information handling procedures can work.
questions.remediation: Establish suitable procedures for protecting relevant intellectual property rights.

questions.prompt: Is use of third-party software and material supported by the relevant rights or permissions?
questions.help: Open-source terms, licences, permissions or applicable exceptions may matter. If none is used, explain how the process would establish rights before use rather than declaring the whole control irrelevant.
questions.remediation: Verify rights or permissions for third-party software and materials.

questions.prompt: Is use of licensed or otherwise restricted material kept within its applicable terms?
questions.help: Consider deployment counts, copying, distribution or other restrictions where applicable. A licence purchase alone may not demonstrate compliance with its terms.
questions.remediation: Address use that exceeds applicable rights or restrictions.

A.5.33.title: Business record protection
A.5.33.objective: Understand whether business records remain protected and usable through their required lifecycle.

questions.prompt: Are protection and retention needs determined for relevant business records?
questions.help: Consider business needs and applicable obligations for each record category. No universal retention period or required record-system product is introduced.
questions.remediation: Determine relevant record protection and retention needs.

questions.prompt: Are business records protected against inappropriate loss or destruction?
questions.help: Use availability and preservation safeguards suited to the records and medium. Existing storage and recovery arrangements can work.
questions.remediation: Protect relevant records against loss, improper change and access.

questions.prompt: Are records protected against unauthorized alteration or falsification?
questions.help: Consider integrity safeguards appropriate to the record system or paper process. No particular immutability product is required.
questions.remediation: Protect records against unauthorized alteration or falsification.

questions.prompt: Are records protected against unauthorized access or release?
questions.help: Apply access and disclosure controls suited to record sensitivity. Restricting disposal alone does not protect disclosure.
questions.remediation: Protect records against unauthorized access or release.

questions.prompt: Are records retained for the periods identified as necessary?
questions.help: Include applicable preservation or hold requirements. This inquiry sets no universal retention period.
questions.remediation: Apply record retention and authorized disposal requirements.

questions.prompt: Is record disposal authorized and carried out in accordance with the applicable requirements?
questions.help: Check whether holds or other obligations prevent disposal. This interview provides no automatic deletion instruction.
questions.remediation: Apply appropriate authorization and safeguards to record disposal.

questions.prompt: Can retained records be retrieved and understood for their intended use?
questions.help: Consider access to the format, required context and appropriate preservation. A stored file that cannot be read or located may not meet the retention need.
questions.remediation: Keep required retained records retrievable and usable.

A.5.34.title: Personal-data safeguards
A.5.34.objective: Understand whether privacy responsibilities and safeguards reflect the organization's actual personal-information processing.

questions.prompt: Have activities involving personal information in this scope been identified?
questions.help: Consider workforce, customer and other data, including provider processing. A data inventory, assessed flows or equivalent approach can work; absence of customer data alone does not mean absence of personal information.
questions.remediation: Identify relevant personal-information processing activities.

questions.prompt: Are applicable privacy and personal-information protection requirements identified for those activities?
questions.help: Use relevant legal, contractual and other commitments with appropriate advice. Do not assume consent is the required basis for all processing.
questions.remediation: Identify applicable privacy and personal-information protection requirements.

questions.prompt: Is responsibility for addressing the identified privacy requirements assigned?
questions.help: An appropriate existing role can work. A named data protection officer is required only where an applicable obligation makes it necessary.
questions.remediation: Assign responsibility for applicable personal-information protection requirements.

questions.prompt: Are safeguards applied to personal-information handling in line with the identified requirements?
questions.help: Consider actual collection, access, sharing and retention needs. Provider processing remains part of the relationship to assess, rather than an automatic exclusion.
questions.remediation: Apply suitable safeguards to actual personal-information handling.

A.5.35.title: Independent security evaluation
A.5.35.objective: Understand whether an independent, competent review evaluates the security approach and its implementation.

questions.prompt: Does the independent review cover the relevant security approach and its implementation?
questions.help: Consider people, processes and technology relevant to the scope. An internal audit or other appropriate review may contribute if coverage fits; its name alone does not establish adequacy.
questions.remediation: Establish appropriate coverage for independent security evaluation.

questions.prompt: Is the reviewer sufficiently independent of the work being evaluated?
questions.help: An internal person outside the reviewed responsibility or an external reviewer may be suitable. Identify conflicts rather than assuming an external contract guarantees independence.
questions.remediation: Arrange review with supported independence from the assessed work.

questions.prompt: Does the reviewer have suitable competence for the evaluation?
questions.help: Relevant experience or expertise may be sufficient; no particular certificate or professional title is imposed.
questions.remediation: Arrange appropriate competence for the security review.

questions.prompt: Are independent reviews performed at the organization's planned intervals?
questions.help: Use the organization's selected timing and rationale. This introduces no annual or quarterly minimum.
questions.remediation: Carry out independent reviews at suitable planned intervals and significant-change triggers.

questions.prompt: Are independent reviews reconsidered when significant changes affect the security approach?
questions.help: Consider changes that could alter the suitability of earlier conclusions. A scheduled review alone may miss a material change.
questions.remediation: Reconsider independent review needs after significant changes.

questions.prompt: Are review results considered and material weaknesses assigned for follow-up?
questions.help: Use existing findings and improvement processes. A completed assessment does not by itself demonstrate that weaknesses were addressed.
questions.remediation: Consider independent review results and follow up material weaknesses.

A.5.36.title: Security-rule adherence
A.5.36.objective: Understand whether practices are checked against the organization's own security rules and departures receive a response.

questions.prompt: Are the security policies, rules and standards relevant to each area understood by the people checking adherence?
questions.help: Use the organization's actual adopted requirements. A generic external checklist alone may not test the rules people must follow.
questions.remediation: Identify applicable internal security rules for adherence checks.

questions.prompt: Is adherence to those rules reviewed through suitable checks of actual practice?
questions.help: Sampling, configuration checks, manager review or other proportionate methods can work. This question imposes no universal frequency or tool.
questions.remediation: Review actual practice against relevant security rules.

questions.prompt: Are departures investigated and given an appropriate corrective or authorized exception response?
questions.help: An exception needs a justified decision; repeated exceptions can signal a rule or implementation problem. Risk acceptance does not automatically establish compliance.
questions.remediation: Investigate departures and follow through on correction or justified exceptions.

A.5.37.title: Operating instructions
A.5.37.objective: Understand whether documented procedures allow people to perform relevant security-sensitive operations consistently.

questions.prompt: Are procedures documented for operational activities that need consistent and safe execution?
questions.help: Consider relevant routine and exceptional tasks. Existing controlled instructions can work; documentation should fit the operation rather than use a prescribed title.
questions.remediation: Document suitable procedures for relevant operational activities.

questions.prompt: Do procedures provide enough information for the intended operators to carry out the work safely?
questions.help: Appropriate prerequisites, key steps and handling of problems can help. A particular template or exhaustive click-by-click script is optional.
questions.remediation: Resolve gaps that prevent safe, consistent execution from the procedures.

questions.prompt: Are current procedures available to the people who need them?
questions.help: Include substitute operators and provider personnel where relevant. Access should be appropriate to the sensitivity of the instructions.
questions.remediation: Make current procedures appropriately accessible to relevant operators.

A.6.1.title: Pre-employment checks
A.6.1.objective: Understand whether personnel screening is lawful, proportionate and performed for relevant roles.

questions.prompt: Are screening checks proportionate to the role's security risks?
questions.help: Consider the information accessed and responsibilities involved. Identical checks for every role can miss relevant differences.
questions.remediation: Define lawful, proportionate screening suited to role risk.

questions.prompt: Are screening arrangements consistent with applicable legal and ethical constraints?
questions.help: Use appropriate advice for the jurisdiction and relationship. Universal criminal, credit or social-media checks are not assumed; do not collect unnecessary sensitive details.
questions.remediation: Align screening arrangements with applicable legal and ethical constraints.

questions.prompt: Are appropriate screening checks completed before the person takes on the relevant role?
questions.help: Include the relevant employment or engagement arrangement. Use minimized completion evidence rather than sensitive screening results in this interview.
questions.remediation: Complete appropriate screening before relevant role engagement.

questions.prompt: Are relevant personnel supplied by a contractor, agency or other outside organization?
questions.help: Provider personnel with relevant responsibilities or access remain relevant to screening arrangements. Not relevant here requires a reason and affects only the supplier-personnel inquiry.

questions.prompt: Are appropriate screening responsibilities for those personnel agreed and supported by suitable assurance?
questions.help: Provider confirmation or other proportionate assurance may work. Do not demand unnecessary sensitive background results merely because screening is outsourced.
questions.remediation: Clarify supplier screening responsibilities and obtain suitable assurance.

questions.prompt: Is there an approach to repeat or update screening where changed risk or applicable requirements warrant it?
questions.help: Use role, risk and legal constraints to decide when further checks are appropriate. No universal rescreening frequency is introduced.
questions.remediation: Define appropriate ongoing screening triggers and responsibilities.

A.6.2.title: Employment security commitments
A.6.2.objective: Understand whether employment or engagement terms clearly establish both parties' security responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Do relevant employment or engagement terms set out the person's security responsibilities?
questions.help: Contracts or incorporated, accessible terms can work. Include obligations appropriate to the work and information accessed; a particular agreement title is optional.
questions.remediation: Establish appropriate personnel security responsibilities in relevant terms.

questions.prompt: Do those terms establish the organization's relevant security responsibilities toward the person?
questions.help: Consider the actual employment or engagement relationship and applicable obligations. Security terms should not present the person's responsibilities as the whole arrangement.
questions.remediation: Clarify the organization's relevant security responsibilities in the arrangement.

questions.prompt: Are the relevant security terms communicated and agreed before they need to be relied on?
questions.help: Acknowledged contracts or another valid agreement route can work. Ask about understanding and agreement rather than treating an unsigned template as implementation.
questions.remediation: Communicate and establish agreement to applicable security terms.

A.6.3.title: Workforce security learning
A.6.3.objective: Understand whether relevant people receive security awareness and role-suited education and training.

questions.prompt: Are security learning needs identified for personnel and relevant interested parties?
questions.help: Consider employees, contractors and provider personnel where their responsibilities affect security. Do not automatically exclude people because they lack an employee record.
questions.remediation: Identify relevant audiences and their security learning needs.

questions.prompt: Do relevant people receive awareness information about the security rules and issues affecting their work?
questions.help: Onboarding, briefings, written updates or other effective methods can work. Content should reflect the organization and changed needs.
questions.remediation: Deliver relevant security awareness information and updates.

questions.prompt: Do people receive education or training suited to their security responsibilities?
questions.help: Different roles may need different learning, such as administrators or incident responders. Existing instruction and practical training can work without a commercial platform.
questions.remediation: Provide learning suited to people's security responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Are missed learning needs or lack of understanding identified and addressed?
questions.help: Completion information, conversations or exercises may help. Attendance alone is limited evidence of understanding; this is a practical follow-up inquiry.
questions.remediation: Address missed learning and understanding gaps.

A.6.4.title: Disciplinary handling
A.6.4.objective: Understand whether security violations can be addressed through a defined and communicated disciplinary process.

questions.prompt: Is a disciplinary process established for relevant security violations?
questions.help: Use the organization's lawful personnel process, including applicable contractual arrangements. No universal sanction or automatic dismissal rule is introduced.
questions.remediation: Establish an appropriate process for addressing security violations.

questions.prompt: Are affected personnel informed of that process?
questions.help: Accessible terms, onboarding communication or another suitable method can work. A procedure held only by HR may not communicate the expectations.
questions.remediation: Communicate the applicable disciplinary process to affected people.

questions.prompt: Are responsibilities established for handling security violation cases consistently and appropriately?
questions.help: Consider evidence, context and applicable personnel rules before decisions. If no cases exist, describe the established process; minimize personal case details.
questions.remediation: Clarify responsibility and appropriate decision handling for security violations.

A.6.5.title: Departure and role-change duties
A.6.5.objective: Understand whether security responsibilities after employment ends or changes are defined, communicated and supported.

questions.prompt: Are security duties that continue after employment ends or changes identified?
questions.help: Confidentiality, information return and intellectual-property obligations may be relevant. Use applicable terms and facts rather than inventing lifelong duties.
questions.remediation: Identify applicable security duties that continue after employment or role changes.

questions.prompt: Are continuing duties communicated to the affected people and relevant parties?
questions.help: Departure or transfer communication can work. Include providers or managers who need to coordinate the change where relevant.
questions.remediation: Communicate continuing duties during departures and role changes.

questions.prompt: Are security responsibilities handed over or reassigned when employment or duties change?
questions.help: Coordinate with access removal and asset return as relevant, while keeping those controls separate. No mandatory departure checklist title is assumed.
questions.remediation: Reassign or hand over security responsibilities affected by departure or role change.

questions.prompt: Are appropriate arrangements established to uphold continuing security obligations?
questions.help: Use lawful agreements and follow-up arrangements. The organization should know how to respond to a breach without assuming legal enforceability from a signature alone.
questions.remediation: Establish appropriate arrangements for upholding continuing security obligations.

A.6.6.title: Confidentiality commitments
A.6.6.objective: Understand whether confidentiality commitments are identified, recorded, accepted and maintained for relevant people.

questions.prompt: Are confidentiality commitments determined from the information people can access and its protection needs?
questions.help: Consider employees and relevant external personnel. Existing employment or service terms can cover suitable commitments; a separate NDA for everyone is not assumed.
questions.remediation: Identify appropriate confidentiality commitments for relevant information access.

questions.prompt: Are those confidentiality commitments documented with an appropriate scope?
questions.help: Consider protected information, permitted use and relevant continuing duties. Use terms suited to the relationship rather than an unexplained template.
questions.remediation: Document confidentiality commitments suited to the relationship and information.

questions.prompt: Have the relevant people agreed to the required confidentiality commitments?
questions.help: A signed agreement or applicable acknowledged contract terms may work. Determine what establishes valid acceptance in the arrangement; a blank form does not.
questions.remediation: Establish appropriate agreement to required confidentiality commitments.

questions.prompt: Are confidentiality arrangements reviewed for continued suitability?
questions.help: Consider planned reviews and changed relationships, information or obligations. No universal renewal or review interval is introduced.
questions.remediation: Review confidentiality arrangements and resolve outdated coverage.

A.6.7.title: Remote-work safeguards
A.6.7.objective: Understand whether remote working is governed and relevant information and assets are protected away from the normal workplace.

questions.prompt: Are security arrangements established for permitted or proposed remote working?
questions.help: Existing acceptable-use or work arrangements can work. If remote work is not permitted, explain how that boundary is established; this does not set native SoA applicability.
questions.remediation: Establish appropriate security arrangements for permitted or proposed remote work.

questions.prompt: Is remote working performed for activities in this scope?
questions.help: Include home, travel and relevant provider personnel working remotely. Outsourcing does not by itself justify Not relevant here. Give a reason for that answer; only the following safeguards are conditional.

questions.prompt: Are information and assets protected from physical exposure in actual remote workspaces?
questions.help: Consider screens, conversations, paper, device custody and household or public access as relevant. Existing workspace rules or assessed arrangements can work.
questions.remediation: Address physical exposure of information and assets in remote workspaces.

questions.prompt: Are devices and locally held information used for remote work appropriately protected?
questions.help: Use safeguards suited to managed or authorized personal devices, where permitted. A specific endpoint or monitoring product is not required.
questions.remediation: Apply suitable protections to remote-work devices and information.

questions.prompt: Are remote connections and access paths protected for the work being performed?
questions.help: Approved access methods, appropriate authentication and protected communication can work. A VPN is one possible method rather than a universal requirement.
questions.remediation: Protect relevant remote access and communication paths.

A.6.8.title: Workforce event reporting
A.6.8.objective: Understand whether people can promptly report observed or suspected security events through a usable route.

questions.prompt: Is a reporting route available for observed or suspected security events?
questions.help: A known contact, service desk, telephone route or other usable channel can work. Include relevant personnel working remotely or through providers.
questions.remediation: Provide an accessible route for reporting suspected or observed security events.

questions.prompt: Do relevant people know what to report and how to use that route?
questions.help: Explain how to report uncertainty without requiring staff to diagnose an incident themselves. Existing awareness or role instructions can communicate the route.
questions.remediation: Communicate what to report and how to reach the reporting route.

questions.prompt: Are people instructed and enabled to report security events promptly?
questions.help: The route should not force people to wait for a routine meeting or complete a technical investigation first. A universal minutes-or-hours deadline is not introduced.
questions.remediation: Enable prompt reporting of observed or suspected security events.

questions.prompt: Can reported events reach the people responsible for assessing and acting on them?
questions.help: A demonstration or actual received report can support the answer. The receiving route should remain usable when normal work tools are affected.
questions.remediation: Ensure reported security events reach responsible assessors.

A.7.1.title: Protected site boundaries
A.7.1.objective: Understand whether physical boundaries protect the information and assets inside the assessed locations.

questions.prompt: Are the boundaries of protected areas clear and matched to where sensitive information and equipment actually sit?
questions.help: Consider offices, storage, shared buildings and provider locations in scope. A floor plan, marked area or practical walkthrough can explain the boundary.
questions.remediation: Align the protected boundary with the sensitive locations and assets.

questions.prompt: Do the physical barriers make unauthorized crossing of that boundary difficult enough for the assessed risks?
questions.help: Explain doors, walls, reception arrangements or equivalent barriers, including shared routes. Choose protection for the actual exposure rather than assuming every site needs fences or guards.
questions.remediation: Strengthen exposed boundary points using proportionate physical safeguards.

questions.prompt: Are damaged or bypassed boundary protections identified and put right?
questions.help: Describe how propped doors, broken locks or changed layouts are noticed and handled. A walkthrough or local reporting arrangement may work; no fixed inspection interval is imposed.
questions.remediation: Resolve degraded protections and keep the boundary aligned with site changes.

A.7.2.title: Controlled site entry
A.7.2.objective: Understand whether physical entry to protected areas follows current authorization and controlled visitor or delivery arrangements.

questions.prompt: Is entry permission limited to people who have a current reason to enter the protected area?
questions.help: Explain approval and the permitted areas for workers and relevant external people. A maintained list, controlled keys or another effective arrangement may be used.
questions.remediation: Limit entry rights to approved people and the areas they need.

questions.prompt: Are physical entry rights removed when the need ends?
questions.help: Consider leavers, role changes and lost keys or credentials. Check the actual removal of access rather than only an update to a staff list.
questions.remediation: Remove obsolete entry rights and address affected credentials.

questions.prompt: Is authorization checked at the routes into protected areas?
questions.help: Consider normal doors and alternate routes, including access from public or shared space. Locks, reception checks or electronic controls may be appropriate; a badge system is not the only solution.
questions.remediation: Close entry routes that bypass the intended authorization check.

questions.prompt: Are visitors kept within the areas and activities they are allowed to access?
questions.help: Explain how a visitor is identified, approved and supervised as needed for the site's exposure. If no visit has occurred, describe the ready procedure rather than inventing a visitor record.
